💡 Key Takeaways
  • A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.
  • It has been revealed that the image shows the Didymos double asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos.
  • The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.

It has been revealed that the image shows the Didymos double asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos.

The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system.

Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth.

For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth.

According to recent reports, but more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid, meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet.

Industry observers note that hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

#105076. Breaking: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1020 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death.
  • It has been revealed that sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals.
  • It has been revealed that now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death. Instead, its extraordinary shape was completely natural and may represent the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a mammal.

It has been revealed that sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals. While most vertebrates have bodies and skulls that are roughly symmetrical on both sides, toothed whales have evolved uneven skull structures to accommodate specialized organs responsible for producing sound and navigating through echolocation.

It has been revealed that now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level. Named Scaphokogia huachafo, the whale lived during the Late Miocene, between 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago, and measured approximately 2.7 meters in length. Its fossilized skull displays the most extreme facial asymmetry known in any whale or dolphin, and possibly in any mammal.

A Prehistoric Whale With an Extraordinary Skull.

"Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked," explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that benites-Palomino investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich's Department of Paleontology. He is currently an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

Sources indicate that the whale's extraordinary appearance also inspired its scientific name. The word huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and is commonly used to describe something excessively flashy, bizarre, extravagant, or even tacky.

"In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant or difficult to categorize aesthetically," says Benites-Palomino.

"When we looked at the proportions of this whale - with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout - it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.".

Scientists Initially Suspected the Skull Was Deformed.

The remarkable fossil was originally recovered during the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru. This desert region is famous among paleontologists for its exceptionally preserved fossils of ancient marine animals.

Benites-Palomino first encountered the specimen in 2015 while preparing his Bachelor's thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its dramatically uneven shape immediately raised an vital question: Was the skull genuinely this crooked when the whale was alive, or had millions of years of geological pressure distorted it?

"The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy - that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years," says Benites-Palomino.

Industry observers note that "But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.".

The findings confirmed that the extraordinary asymmetry was part of the whale's natural anatomy, rather than damage caused by burial, fossilization, or disease.

A Bizarre Adaptation for Hunting Along the Seafloor.

Industry observers note that the whale's unusual skull also offers clues about how it survived. Modern sperm whales typically pursue squid in deep ocean waters, but Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have followed a very different hunting strategy. Its anatomy suggests that it was highly adapted to searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal waters.

One of its most distinctive features was a large, tube-shaped snout strengthened by dense bone and cartilage that had hardened into bone. These heavy structures served as natural ballast, moving the whale's center of gravity forward and downward.

Industry observers note that its snout also pointed downward at an angle of 31 degrees relative to the rest of its skull. By reconstructing the joint connecting the skull to the first neck vertebra, known as the atlas, scientists determined that Scaphokogia could bend its head downward by as much as 55 degrees.

"The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom," explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, co-author of the study and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich.

"The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.".

In a recent development, researchers also believe the whale may have relied on its highly specialized echolocation system to locate prey beneath the soft sediment of coastal environments. Unlike other marine mammals that forage along the ocean floor, Scaphokogia lacked the sensitive facial whiskers or specialized visual adaptations that can help animals find food near the bottom.

Instead, its extraordinarily asymmetrical skull may have supported a sophisticated biological sonar system that allowed it to detect hidden prey.

In a recent development, this unusual feeding strategy represents a specialized way of life that no longer exists among modern marine mammals. As ocean conditions shifted toward the end of the Miocene, the ecological niche occupied by Scaphokogia disappeared, eventually giving way to the marine mammal communities familiar today.

The discovery provides a remarkable glimpse into how far evolution once pushed the anatomy of whales, producing a creature whose dramatically crooked face was not a deformity, but an adaptation to a vanished underwater world.

Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists.

Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.

At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning Â£325,000 a week at Chelsea.

"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," remarked then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a Â£50m deal in 2022.

"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.

"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us.".

Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal, and commanded combined transfer fees of about Â£100m.

But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May.

The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

How Sterling went from England star to court appearance.

Sterling's life was touched by tragedy at a young age.

Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead.

His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money.

Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems.

In a recent development, in an interview with the Players' Tribune, external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem.".

He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison.".

Sterling would grow to become one of the standout English attacking talents of his generation.

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash.

Raheem Sterling: From school struggles to a class of his own.

On 14 November 2012 - aged 17 years and 342 days - Sterling made his England debut on the night his Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard won his 100th cap in a 4-2 defeat by Sweden in Stockholm.

Sterling would go on to make 81 more appearances for his country, scoring 20 goals.

He featured at three World Cups - 2014, 2018 and 2022 - and two European Championships. He was one of the standout players as England reached the Euro 2020 final at Wembley, where they were beaten by Italy.

Sterling was now at the peak of his career - the former Queens Park Rangers youngster, who has a tattoo on his forearm of a young boy holding a football looking up at the Wembley arch, named in the team of the tournament by Uefa.

Liverpool had signed a 15-year-old Sterling from QPR for Â£600,000 in February 2010.

He made his senior Reds debut two years later and became the second-youngest goalscorer in their history - behind Michael Owen - when he scored the winner against Reading in October 2012 at the age of 17.

In 2015, Sterling joined Manchester City in a deal worth up to Â£49m, making him the most expensive English player at the time.

He had been under contract at Anfield until 2017 but turned down a upcoming deal to move to Liverpool's rivals, with City boss Manuel Pellegrini describing the 20-year-old as "one of the best attacking players in world football".

Sterling went on to score 131 goals in 339 appearances in all competitions during seven successful years at Etihad Stadium.

As well as four Premier League titles, he helped City win five League Cups, one FA Cup and one Community Shield.

It was while he was at City, in 2021, that Sterling became an MBE in the Queen's Birthday Honours for his services to racial equality in sport.

In a recent development, "I am grateful to have been recognised," he mentioned. "But my priority is to try to help to educate society and myself. I'm learning every day.".

After City came the move to Chelsea, where his career began to stall.

Tuchel, now England manager, was sacked two months after signing Sterling, who made just 45 Premier League starts for the Blues over four years.

Off the pitch, he released a scholarship fund aimed at closing the gap in the number of black British students who go to university.

On the pitch, he was finding it a struggle.

He spent 18 months as a member of Chelsea's so-called 'bomb squad', and a season-long loan to Arsenal in 2024-25 proved largely unsuccessful.

Sterling: If you grew up in a certain area you feel like there's limits.

'Sterling will look back and wonder'.

As well as his success on the field, Sterling has made headlines off it too.

In 2015, when he was 20, reports began to surface about his behaviour away from the game.

Sterling was pictured apparently inhaling nitrous oxide and was also photographed smoking a shisha pipe.

That prompted then Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers to warn Sterling he would "look back in 20 years and wonder what he was doing".

Sterling also made headlines while on duty for England at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

The Sun ran a story titled "Raheem shoots himself in the foot" as pictures emerged of a tattoo of an M16 assault rifle on his leg.

Sterling explained on social media: "When I was 2 my father died from being gunned down to death I made a promise to myself I would never touch a gun in my life time. I shoot with my right foot so it has a deeper meaning.".

The incident led to a widespread discussion in the UK about the treatment of black athletes in the media, with comparisons drawn between how Sterling's life was covered compared to others.

Sterling spoke out a number of times on the concern and wider racism in society, which was reflected in him being made an MBE.

According to recent reports, five years after his MBE, Sterling's career has stalled. He has not played since appearing for Feyenoord on 17 May, after agreeing a short-term move to the Netherlands.

Eleven days after that game, he was arrested after crashing a Lamborghini near the M3 in Hampshire.

Watch: Sterling joins PL 100 club - best goals & stats.

Listen: From Wembley schoolboy to playing for England at Wembley.

Sterling was riding the crest of a wave when he moved from Manchester City to Chelsea in the summer of 2022 for Â£50m.

His medal cabinet was already fit to burst with 10 major trophies under Guardiola and, alongside Harry Kane, he was arguably England's most key player for then head coach Gareth Southgate.

Tuchel viewed Sterling as his number one target that summer and Chelsea's new ownership - Behdad Eghbali and Todd Boehly - delivered as the club entered the post-Roman Abramovich era.

Two months later, Tuchel was sacked and Graham Potter was in situ.

Sterling's career has not been the same since.

It is, of course, senseless to suggest the troubles Sterling has had on and off the pitch in recent years are simply down to the sacking of Tuchel in 2022.

But speak to those close to Sterling and they will explain Tuchel was among the key factors behind the winger's decision to swap Manchester for west London.

He was captivated by Tuchel's vision, not only for the team, but his role in it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0).

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics.

Industry observers note that the question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is vital because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” states Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

Recent findings suggest that mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late 1700s (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

In a recent development, in Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, indicates maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

Industry observers note that if true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” states Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

In his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing latest techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

It has been revealed that riemann then indicated that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the organization. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance noted in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance remarked auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says.

Trading in the organization’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog rolled out an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

Daniella—earning her second Mirrorball following her victory with Iman Shumpert in season 30—added, "I'm just so freaking grateful.".

Of course, the 2026 champions achieving the sole purpose of the competition meant they outscored runner-up Amber Glenn, as well as Connor Wood, Tatyana Ali and Maura Higgins.

It has been revealed that in a salsa danced to "Danza Kuduro," Ezra and Daniella set the stage on fire. To switch things up, the runner also landed an empowering freestyle to "Numb" by Linkin Park, which Daniella teased on the show's official podcast Nov. 19 would include moves that have "definitely never been done before," like Ezra beginning the routine without his prosthetic.

After putting on the device mid-routine, it unsuctioned later in the dance, but he was able to make an impressive recovery, with Derek raving, "The worst-case scenario might have happened and you wouldn't even have known, the way you rose in that moment.".

Meanwhile, Amber and partner Pasha Pashkov moved their feet to a quickstep set to "Sing Sing Sing" by Louis Prima, complemented by a colorful freestyle to Madonna hits "Like a Prayer" and "Music.".

Wood led pro Rylee Arnold in an emotional Viennese Waltz, in addition to a freestyle mashing up "Singin’ in the Rain" and Rihanna's "Umbrella." They were joined by Rylee's sister, Lindsay Arnold Cusick, for the routine after the former pro stepped away from the show in 2021.

Recent findings suggest that love Island's Higgins tangoed with Mark Ballas, then balancing out the spicy number with a jazzy rendition of "Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend" featuring Irish folk song selections as a nod to her heritage. And Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik delivered the night's third tango, as well as a jazzy freestyle to a Judy Garland song that was out of this world.

Amber, Ezra and Maura all received perfect scores of 90 while Connor and Tatyana received 82 points from the judges.

According to recent reports, still, all of the finalists were surrounded by support from their previously eliminated castmates taking one more spin around the ballroom. Their return reminded viewers of the year's shocking twists and turns that sent home top performers like Harry Shum Jr., Jenna Dewan and Taylor Hanson despite their consistently positive feedback from the judges' panel.

On the other foot, stars like Julia Stiles and Ciara Miller—whose claim to fame in the competition became their heartfelt connection with partners Ezra Sosa and Brandon Armstrong, respectively—delighted the audience by coming in all smiles following their emotional eliminations.

Sources indicate that that mentioned, while only one winner can take home the title, DWTS has changed the lives of many of its alums. Read on for more secrets about the ABC series.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones noted he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality remarked on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last.".

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show.".

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

According to recent reports, "You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody.".

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

According to recent reports, "If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together.".

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

That doesn't appear to be the case.

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay noted on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'".

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

In a recent development, "They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner.".

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well.".

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again.".

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers.".

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that if you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee noted pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting.".

A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal.
  • The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB).
  • According to recent reports, first discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal. A new study published in Nature dates the ancient remains to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and suggests that the human family tree in southern Africa was much more complicated than previously believed.

The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB). The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how early human relatives evolved and how different species were related.

According to recent reports, first discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity. It also became the original "type specimen" used to define the species Australopithecus africanus. However, scientists never established definitive criteria for assigning later fossil discoveries to this species. As a result, the Taung Child remains the only fossil that can be identified with certainty as Australopithecus africanus.

"For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," says Professor Gabriele Macho. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk -- it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.".

Ancient Fossils Reveal a More Complex Human Family Tree.

To investigate how the Taung Child compared with other early human relatives, researchers examined tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development during growth. They found that several adult fossils traditionally classified as Australopithecus africanus followed developmental patterns that differed from those of the Taung Child.

Differences in brain development were particularly revealing. They suggest that fossils previously grouped into a single species may actually represent several distinct hominin species that inhabited the Sterkfontein region, either at the same time or during different periods.

These findings raise vital questions about the diversity of our ancient ancestors and suggest that early human evolution followed a much more complicated path than scientists once assumed.

How Climate Change Shaped Human Evolution.

The researchers believe that dramatic environmental changes played a major role in creating this evolutionary diversity. Millions of years ago, southern Africa experienced repeated shifts between wetter and drier climates, continually transforming the landscape and the habitats available to early human relatives.

As suitable environments expanded and contracted, ancient hominin populations moved with them. Some groups became geographically isolated and evolved along different paths, while others eventually came back into contact and interbred. These changing conditions also exposed populations to different predators and pathogens, creating additional pressures that shaped their evolution.

Southern Africa's position along the boundary between tropical and temperate ecosystems made it especially notable in this process. Over thousands of years, shifting habitats may have repeatedly brought different hominin species together, creating opportunities for interbreeding and hybridization.

A Greener South Africa 3 Million Years Ago.

The study also reveals a surprising picture of the environment in which the Taung Child lived. Evidence preserved in fossilized pollen indicates that the region was once considerably wetter and more heavily forested than it is today.

Researchers identified evidence of tree species that are now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast, suggesting that the landscape surrounding the Taung Child was dramatically different from modern South Africa.

Together, these discoveries challenge the traditional view of human evolution as a relatively straightforward progression from one species to another. Instead, they point to a shifting network of populations that repeatedly separated, adapted, reunited, and sometimes interbred as environmental conditions changed.

Industry observers note that more than 100 years after its discovery, the Taung Child is once again transforming our understanding of human origins. Its latest secrets suggest that the emergence of our own genus, Homo, was preceded by a far more diverse and interconnected world of ancient human relatives than previously recognized.

Confusion and anger - Yoro red card rescinded, but row goes on

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leny Yoro will be available for Manchester United's game against Brentford on Saturday after his one-match ban was rescinded.
  • Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.
  • Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leny Yoro will be available for Manchester United's game against Brentford on Saturday after his one-match ban was rescinded.

Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.

Let's recap what happened on Sunday.

Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.

Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.

It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?

Then came the events of Tuesday.

First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.

Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb noted the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.

Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.

But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?

BBC Sport looks at how the system works.

So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?

"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.

It continued a theme from his post-match news conference.

Sources indicate that you can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?

You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.

The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.

In a recent development, as for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.

It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.

Would that change his opinion? Almost certainly not.

According to recent reports, webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.

So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?

It has been revealed that the VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.

It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.

Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.

It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.

But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.

'And the three points?' - Pochettino after Yoro red overturned.

How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.

In a recent development, an FA regulatory commission has mentioned the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.

Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.

And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.

Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.

Sources indicate that but surely the FA is the higher body? Not quite.

The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.

If the Premier League tells Pro Ref the decision is right or wrong, that counts far more than any vote by an FA commission.

So how did United make their case?

BBC Sport understands the club argued that if Isak had maintained his top recorded speed, he would not have got to the ball first.

The club say that is objectively provable, within minutes, using data. This, they say, was not a subjective decision.

To argue it was not subjective goes completely against the nature of the decision - it required a referee's judgement.

Sources indicate that whatever this data was, it most definitely was not available to the referees. The VAR cannot call upon a 3D animation of each player, detailing their running speed and providing an objective result.

Sources indicate that how much stock did the commission place on this evidence? We will not know until the written reasons are published in a few days' time.

But United are not going to let this lie, and Pro Ref is not going to bend.

Such is the way FA commissions work, you can never be sure who will win.

There are three panel members who are usually former players, but occasionally you might get a retired referee.

The role of the commission is not to "usurp the referee by re-refereeing the incident".

A designated referee delegate is present to answer questions on the laws of the game, but they cannot offer an opinion on the incident.

It has been revealed that the only input Pro Ref has is the official's report - a short entry by the referee that indicates which law was used for the red card. There is no other context.

It will read something like this: "I have to report that I, as the referee, sent off Yoro, Leny of Manchester United FC Under Law 12 section: S5.".

The burden is on the club to prove its case by submitting a body of evidence - videos, images and testimony.

In a recent development, there is no right of reply. The evidence is weighed up by the panel, a vote is cast and the majority wins.

It makes predicting the outcome notoriously difficult, as the system is an opinion poll based upon a club trying to persuade at least two people to agree with them.

Take a look at Aston Villa's successful appeal against Douglas Luiz's red card for violent conduct four years ago. Luiz had been sent off via a VAR review for a headbutt on Aleksandar Mitrovic.

The panel's written reasons stated the appeal was won partly because Luiz was "a few inches shorter than Mr Mitrovic so his forehead is naturally at the same height as Mr Mitrovic's nose/face as the two players come together".

Recent findings suggest that so, when the two players bumped chests the headbutt was just an accident. Appeal upheld because Luiz was a bit shorter.

Some might think anything is worth trying.

YunLone Galaxy star projector review — a sub-$30 customizable night light

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coming complete with a smartphone app, the YunLone Galaxy Projector can project just about any color combination you can think of onto the ceiling.
  • Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Sources indicate that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is an inexpensive but effective way to bring the marvel of space into your living room or bedroom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coming complete with a smartphone app, the YunLone Galaxy Projector can project just about any color combination you can think of onto the ceiling. It has a built-in Bluetooth speaker, too, offering all-around relaxation and an ambience setting.

Setting up the app could be simpler.

Lack of buttons on the unit itself.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Sources indicate that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is an inexpensive but effective way to bring the marvel of space into your living room or bedroom. Costing around $28, this star projector can display beautiful dancing auroras across your walls and ceiling, and thanks to app support, a huge range of color options are available. In fact, the color combinations you can display here are almost infinite.

It has been revealed that with built-in sounds, a Bluetooth speaker and endless customization options, this really is an all-singing, all-dancing star projector. We're amazed at just how much is loaded into this package for such a low price. It's surprisingly good quality, too, with the unit itself being sturdy and made out of hard-wearing plastic.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't a scientific star projector, of course. For that, we'd recommend the Sega Toys Homestar Classic or the Hommkiety Galaxy Projector. But even though the YunLone Galaxy Projector won't give you an accurate view of the Northern Hemisphere's night sky or a close-up of the moon, it's still a projector we recommend. If you're looking to create a relaxing atmosphere, it's one of the best star projectors we've reviewed.

In a recent development, the YunLone Galaxy Projector doesn't have the most attractive design: It's clearly built for functionality rather than aesthetics. If an aesthetically pleasing projector unit is what you're looking for, perhaps consider the Jiawen Galaxy Projector Light. You won't find nearly as many functions as the YunLone Galaxy Projector packs in, however.

According to recent reports, that isn't to say that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is ugly, though. The design is basic, with a circular shape that houses a clear globe in the middle that acts as the projector. It sits on rubberized feet, so it doesn't easily slip or move around, and it's naturally tilted, so it points slightly diagonally rather than straight up. Given the wide reach of the projector, it helps spread the aurora lights across your entire room.

The projector has a solid build quality: It's plastic but feels sturdy and well-made. If you're buying for a child's bedroom, you don't need to worry about little hands being too rough when using it. Those rubber feet help prevent it from being knocked off a desk or bedside table, too.

Industry observers note that as already mentioned, the YunLone Galaxy Projector isn't a scientific star projector. If you want to recreate actual constellations and close-ups of planets on your bedroom ceiling, this is not the projector for you. But if you're looking for beautiful, mesmerizing aurora-style patterns, it's a great choice.

Recent findings suggest that once you're connected to the app, you can control exactly what colors the projector displays. Not only can you choose from a number of preset arrangements — labeled as seasons, colors or holidays, so you can create a mood that matches the time of year or how you feel — but you can set your own entire color scheme by choosing from a color wheel. You can also set the brightness, whether the lights will have a "breathing" effect, and how fast they ripple across your ceiling.

It's a very neat touch, and it goes beyond what we'd expect to find in a star projector in this price range. If you don't want to bother with app connection, you can still set a range of colors and options from the remote control, but the options here are more limited.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector comes equipped with a laser, so it can project green laser stars onto your walls and ceiling. We didn't love the look of these, though, so it's good that you can turn them off independently of the aurora lights. You can also change the laser's brightness if you'd like the stars to appear dimmer.

Both the laser stars and the aurora projections have a very wide reach, covering most of the walls and ceiling of the bedroom we tested the unit in. Obviously, this will vary depending on the size of your room and how far away from the ceiling/wall you place the unit, but we were pleasantly surprised by the coverage offered by this projector.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector has a companion app that can be downloaded onto an Android or Apple smartphone. Once the app is set up and paired with your unit, you have full control over the colors, speed and brightness of your projections.

The pairing process isn't entirely straightforward, however, with no simple way of forcing the projector to enter pairing mode. The instructions tell you to quickly turn the unit on and off three times, but it took several attempts before we successfully put the projector into pairing mode.

Thankfully, once that's done, it should stay paired with your smartphone permanently so you won't have to repeat the process. And the app itself is very easy to use, working seamlessly to change the colors of the projection unit.

The bundled remote control (which requires two AAA batteries, not included) is a little more complex than most, offering a range of buttons to control both the built-in speaker and the light itself. We'd highly recommend opting for the app option as it gives you much better control over the unit, but if your smartphone is unavailable, you can at least set basic color and speed with the remote.

You can connect a music player to the projector via Bluetooth to play your own audio through its built-in speaker. The quality is decent rather than outstanding: It obviously doesn't match the sound of a specialist speaker, but it's as good as we'd expect any $28 speaker to be. It lacks the bass that music requires to sound "complete" but will be ideal for listening to audiobooks and podcasts.

In a neat touch, the YunLone Galaxy Projector also has eight built-in sound effects, including white noise, waves, lullabies and a storm, which some users may find relaxing and good to fall asleep to.

We have been thoroughly impressed with what the YunLone Galaxy Projector offers. Its projections are beautiful auroras that dance across your ceiling, and the ability to fully customize the color and speed is something that we really didn't expect to find at a $28 price point.

Industry observers note that if you're on a budget and looking for a non-scientific projector to use to relax and unwind with, we really don't think you can find a better unit. If, however, you want something that offers more scientific projections, you'll need to look elsewhere.

Sega Toys' range of projectors, including the Homestar Flux and the Homestar Classic, is excellent but comes with a much bigger price tag. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector is worth considering too, offering realistic projections but with a price tag closer to $50.

According to recent reports, the good thing about these projectors is that they come with interchangeable discs, able to display various images of space. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector has several discs in the box, but you'll need to buy extra discs for the Sega Toys range, so that’s an extra cost to factor in.

Ezra Frech cha-cha'd real smooth past a mishap during the Dancing With the Stars finale.

The Paralympian and pro partner Daniella Karagach sent a powerful message with their freestyle routine to "Numb" by Linkin Park on the Nov. 24 finale, bringing in wheelchair customers and professional dancers Joel Brown and Rafael Castellano as guest stars before taking home the Mirrorball trophy.

Recent findings suggest that but it was also Frech's own flawless recovery that inspired audiences, as the 21-year-old began the poignant performance without his prosthetic leg before putting it on mid-show. However, it unsuctioned during the routine, forcing him to lift Karagach in the air while balancing on one leg.

After the stunning feat, Frech then smoothly reattached his prosthetic and nailed the rest of the choreography, earning perfect 10s from judges Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and Bruno Tonioli.

After cohost Alfonso Ribeiro confirmed Frech's "incredible recovery" was not pre-planned, Hough praised the athlete as a "hero.".

"This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show. What you did tonight was forever," Hough stated. "Kids will look up to you and see what's possible.".

He noted, "The worst-case scenario might have happened, and you wouldn't even have known the way you rose in that moment.".

Tonioli agreed, adding, "What we witnessed tonight goes beyond dancing. This is a powerful, beautiful, life-affirming statement that will inspire the nation and the world.".

So, what happened during the routine?

In a recent development, "The leg unsuctioned, and it came off in the middle of the dance," Frech explained. "But listen, we put our heart, our blood, our sweat, our tears into this.".

He added, "If one person with a disability feels more confident and holds their head up high because of this show, then I've done my job.".

That message of empowerment was the foundation of their performance, as Frech noted in the pre-taped package.

According to recent reports, "I want it to be a celebration of what is possible when you're different," he told Karagach in rehearsal through tears. "What you've done, leaning into my prosthetic, finding such a beautiful way to highlight it and not shy away from it, is unbelievable.".

For their last dance, they picked an anthem from Linkin Park that Frech said is "all about breaking stereotypes.".

"No sob story. This is all about power," he explained. "We're going to be bringing high intensity with talented wheelchair dancers, because we want to change the way people see disability through this dance.".

The number led to Frech and Karagach winning season 35, with him becoming the first Paralympian to take home the Mirrorball, as well as the first amputee and youngest male winner.

As Frech put it, "This is the most special moment of my life.".

For a deeper dive on the rhythm of Dancing With the Stars, read on.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Sources indicate that citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones stated he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last.".

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show.".

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Industry observers note that similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody.".

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—claims the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

Sources indicate that "If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together.".

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

That doesn't appear to be the case.

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'".

In fact, Jenna noted the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna mentioned on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner.".

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

In a recent development, "It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well.".

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Sources indicate that put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again.".

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers.".

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that if you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and latest in something different every week, so it stays interesting.".

Breaking: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to fresh findings shared with WIRED.
  • The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk.
  • In a recent development, “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to fresh findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

In a recent development, “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” claims Greg Pollock, the director of research at security firm UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”.

Recent findings suggest that the two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

It has been revealed that exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more crucial than ever to attackers.

It has been revealed that the data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock indicates.

The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He states the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

In a recent development, pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, says that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.

“Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he says. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”.

The larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler says.

It has been revealed that “After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how big it was.”.

According to recent reports, fowler claims there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.

Recent findings suggest that fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting firm, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.

Recent findings suggest that the enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the Pan American Health Organization revealed the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking newly introduced ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

In a recent development, the Pan American Health Organization revealed the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking newly introduced ones.

Sources indicate that "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in Newly introduced York and two in Wisconsin.

Sources indicate that the commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas noted during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, stated Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action proposal in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

Industry observers note that CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz remarked in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

In a recent development, last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

Recent findings suggest that "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy noted. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

In a recent development, CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

Industry observers note that the MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC demonstrates that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood remarked in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

Recent findings suggest that "We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Industry observers note that based on this year's case count, a upcoming tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

Sources indicate that the U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.
