💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a new study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.
  • Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes.
  • It has been revealed that mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a new study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.

Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes. They detected at least one of 19 mycotoxins in every product, and many contained multiple toxins.

It has been revealed that mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds. They can enter the food supply when agricultural crops become contaminated during growing, harvesting, or storage.

The investigation was led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy, with contributions from Cranfield University. The researchers analyzed 212 products, including plant-based meat alternatives (PMBAs) and plant-based beverages (PBBs). The selection covered foods commonly found on supermarket shelves, such as vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond, and soy milk.

It has been revealed that although the findings highlight how widespread these naturally occurring contaminants can be, the researchers also identified an vital reassuring detail. Every product contained mycotoxin concentrations below recommended European Union guideline levels, which the team said reflected the high food quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.

Why Plant-Based Foods Can Contain Fungal Toxins.

It has been revealed that many of the ingredients used to manufacture plant-based foods are particularly susceptible to fungal contamination. Grains, legumes, and seeds can encounter mold in fields or storage facilities, creating opportunities for mycotoxins to develop before the ingredients reach food manufacturers.

Sources indicate that unlike bacteria or viruses, mycotoxins are chemical substances produced by certain fungi. Their presence in food does not necessarily mean the product contains living mold, and detecting a toxin does not automatically mean the food is unsafe. The potential health risk depends on factors such as the type of toxin, its concentration, and how much a person consumes over time.

Industry observers note that this distinction is especially key for people who eat plant-based products frequently. Someone whose diet regularly includes meat substitutes, dairy alternatives, grains, and legumes may encounter these substances through several different foods rather than a single source.

Could Repeated Exposure Pose Health Risks?

While the concentrations detected in the UK products were below recommended EU guidelines, researchers say the potential effects of repeated exposure deserve closer attention.

Earlier studies have suggested that consuming small amounts of mycotoxins regularly may contribute to cumulative exposure and potentially increase health risks. In other words, assessing a single product may not provide a complete picture of a person's overall dietary exposure.

In a recent development, eating one of these products occasionally is unlikely to cause problems based on the levels reported. However, a diet that relies heavily or exclusively on plant-based foods could involve repeated exposure to mycotoxins from numerous ingredients and products. Researchers say understanding the combined effects is important for evaluating possible long-term health consequences.

In a recent development, the severity of mycotoxin exposure varies depending on the compounds involved and the amount consumed. At sufficiently high or harmful exposure levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys, interfere with normal immune system function, and increase the risk of cancer.

Industry observers note that the new findings do not establish that the tested products cause these conditions. Instead, they provide information that scientists can use to estimate how much exposure consumers may receive through their diets and develop more accurate food safety risk assessments for the UK population.

Scientists Call for Better Monitoring of Plant-Based Ingredients.

Andrea Patriarca, Senior Lecturer in Mycology at Cranfield University, emphasized that mycotoxins are a natural part of the food environment and should not discourage people from eating a varied diet. Mycology is the branch of biology devoted to studying fungi, including molds and yeasts.

"Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.

However, a significant concern arises when upcoming foods enter the market, as there are at the moment no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins. We collaborate closely with various sectors in the food industry, from farmers to food companies, to help implement effective mycotoxin management integrated within food safety standards. The data from our research helps food safety organizations in assessing risks, particularly in complex multi-ingredient products.

It has been revealed that we are currently collaborating with the University of Parma to evaluate the risks faced by the population based on different dietary habits. Our aim is to advise policymakers and raise awareness among vulnerable consumers.".

The researchers are particularly interested in how food safety monitoring can keep pace with the growing range of plant-based products. Foods made from multiple ingredients present additional challenges because each component may introduce different contaminants, making overall exposure more difficult to assess.

Their work also underscores the importance of monitoring raw materials throughout the food production process. Identifying and controlling contamination before ingredients are combined into finished products could help manufacturers manage potential risks more effectively.

What the Findings Mean for Plant-Based Diets.

The discovery of fungal toxins in all 212 products highlights the importance of studying dietary exposure across multiple foods, rather than evaluating each product in isolation.

According to recent reports, for consumers, the results are not a reason to abandon vegan or vegetarian foods. The concentrations measured were below recommended EU guidelines, and the researchers stress that mycotoxins cannot be completely eliminated from the food supply.

In a recent development, instead, the study points to the need for continued research into how different eating habits influence exposure, particularly among people who depend heavily on plant-based products. The University of Parma and Cranfield University are continuing their collaboration to investigate these dietary patterns, identify potentially vulnerable groups, and provide evidence that can inform future food safety policies.

The research, titled "Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market," was published in the journal Food Control.

The study was conducted as part of the European Union-funded Horizon Europe FunShield4Med project (HORIZON-WIDERA-2021-ACCESS-03), Grant Agreement No 101079173.

Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?

While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.

"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho stated after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10.".

While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?

BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.

Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.

He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.

He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.

He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.

When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.

He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.

While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.

But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.

It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.

The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.

His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.

The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top.

The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.

However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.

Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.

Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
  • "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar stated, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

It has been revealed that climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

Recent findings suggest that in the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

According to recent reports, while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

Sources indicate that "Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar stated. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

It has been revealed that environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute noted it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky problem. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar noted, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

It has been revealed that carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

It has been revealed that "Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar noted.

Sources indicate that carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die.
  • Fresh observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.
  • According to recent reports, NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper.

Fresh observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.

According to recent reports, NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.".

Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity.

As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf, the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived "red giant" phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris.

In a recent development, during the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space.

Industry observers note that to better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming.

According to recent reports, "Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai mentioned. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.".

Sources indicate that the team was able to determine that this gas shell of IRAS 06530-0213 is around half a light-year wide and was ejected into space around 6,500 years ago. It represents the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before this kind of star enters the final phase of its life.

Industry observers note that the team thinks that for around 2,000 years after the pulse, the star lost mass at a lower rate. This mass loss then increased sharply over the following 1,000 years. This led to the creation of a lumpy shell of gas now seen as a tangle of material filaments around the dying star. The fact that these filaments have a spiral shape could indicate that IRAS 06530-0213 has an unseen partner orbiting it, stirring the gas.

Meanwhile, the hourglass-shaped nebula immediately around the star began to take shape around 700 years ago, meaning that the red giant phase for IRAS 06530-0213 only ended very recently, in cosmic terms at least.

There are also unexpected elements to the ALMA observations of IRAS 06530-0213.

The team discovered an unexpected abundance of heavy versions, or isotopes, of elements like carbon, oxygen and nitrogen around IRAS 06530-0213.

This doesn't conform to models of how stars like IRAS 06530-0213 forge elements and mix them into their surroundings, though similar signatures have been seen around odd stellar objects, with violent bursts of nuclear fusion thought to be the cause.As well as seeing something unexpected, the researchers didn't detect something they expected to observe.

According to recent reports, dying stars like IRAS 06530-0213 have previously been known to have companions, typically sitting with them inside compact disks of dust. These disks are indirect evidence of material being dragged from the close companion star to the dying star. This is a process scientists have used to explain jet-sculpted hourglass shapes.

However, ALMA failed to detect such disk around IRAS 06530. The team suggests that this could be because a disk existed, albeit briefly, during which time it powered a short burst of high-speed jets that helped sculpt the hourglass, following this the disk simply faded away.

"Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres," Sahai concluded. "IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."The team's research was published on Friday (Nov. 20) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, Fresh Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#105058. Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1547 w)

Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments.
  • In experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising new direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a compound that increases the amount of energy the body uses rather than simply reducing how much food a person eats.

In experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass. It also increased energy expenditure by up to 18%, even though the mice did not become more physically active or experience an increase in body temperature.

The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising new direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The experimental compound also appeared to enhance the benefits of popular weight-loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy when the treatments were used together. However, its effectiveness and safety have not yet been established in humans.

A Different Approach to Weight Loss Than Ozempic.

Over the past five years, medications known as GLP-1 drugs have transformed the treatment of obesity and other metabolic conditions, including diabetes and fatty liver disease. Drugs marketed as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound have helped many patients achieve substantial weight loss while improving their ability to regulate blood sugar.

Despite these benefits, the medications have notable limitations. Nausea and other digestive problems can make treatment difficult for some patients. Because these drugs reduce appetite and food consumption, they can also increase the risk of inadequate nutrition and loss of muscle mass. Over time, losing too much muscle can contribute to weakness, frailty, and other health complications.

Berkeley researchers wanted to investigate a fundamentally different strategy. Rather than focusing on reducing calorie intake, they explored whether it would be possible to increase the amount of energy the body burns.

Industry observers note that this process, known as energy expenditure, includes the calories used to maintain basic bodily functions, regulate metabolism, and support everyday activities. Increasing energy expenditure could potentially help people lose weight without relying exclusively on eating less.

"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," said Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second.".

A Compound That Burns Fat While Preserving Muscle.

The researchers focused on a molecule called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA), which has an unusual combination of effects on the body's metabolism.

Recent findings suggest that TOFA interferes with the production of lipids, a broad category of fatty substances that includes cholesterol and triglycerides. These molecules serve important functions, but excessive levels of certain lipids can contribute to metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

At the same time, TOFA activates genes involved in taking up and burning fat for energy. This combination allows the compound to influence both how the body produces fat and how it uses fat as fuel.

In mice, treatment with TOFA produced several encouraging results. The animals became more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Improved insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to control blood sugar, an important benefit for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The compound also lowered triglyceride levels and improved characteristics of fatty liver disease, a condition in which excess fat accumulates inside liver cells and can eventually interfere with liver function.

Perhaps most notably, obese mice treated with TOFA lost weight primarily through reductions in body fat, without experiencing significant losses of lean muscle mass. This distinction could be especially valuable because maintaining muscle is key for strength, mobility, and long-term metabolic health.

How TOFA Increases Energy Burning by 18%.

Although TOFA was originally discovered in the 1970s, the new research uncovered additional properties that could make it particularly useful for treating metabolic disease.

Recent findings suggest that the compound belongs to a group of substances known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds interfere with enzymes that help the body manufacture fatty acids, effectively slowing the production of certain fats.

Other ACC inhibitors have previously advanced to mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic diseases. One major obstacle has been an unexpected side effect: many of these compounds increase triglycerides in the blood, potentially raising the risk of heart problems.

According to recent reports, the Berkeley team discovered that TOFA does more than inhibit ACC. It also activates two cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which help regulate the genes responsible for fat metabolism.

These receptors function as molecular switches. When activated, they stimulate processes that allow cells to absorb fatty acids and break them down to produce energy. In effect, TOFA simultaneously reduces the production of certain fats and encourages the body to burn fat that is already available.

Recent findings suggest that in mice, this activity increased energy expenditure by as much as 18%, without requiring additional physical activity or raising body temperature. Unlike other ACC inhibitors, TOFA also did not cause triglyceride levels to rise, potentially because of its additional effects on fat metabolism.

Sources indicate that "TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," mentioned study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively.".

Sources indicate that to understand whether these effects could be reproduced with separate treatments, the scientists gave mice a combination of two different compounds. One blocked lipid production, while the other stimulated energy expenditure.

According to recent reports, surprisingly, this two-compound approach was less effective at improving overall metabolic health than TOFA alone. The finding suggests that TOFA's ability to influence multiple metabolic processes through a single molecule may be an vital part of its effectiveness.

Could TOFA Make Ozempic and Wegovy More Effective?

The researchers also investigated whether TOFA could improve the results of existing GLP-1 medications.

They tested the compound alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro and Zepbound.

In a recent development, these medications primarily help people lose weight by reducing appetite and food intake. TOFA, by contrast, targets the other side of the energy balance equation by increasing how much energy the body expends.

When the researchers combined TOFA with these medications in mice, the results were more favorable than those produced by either treatment alone. The combinations led to greater improvements in body weight, blood glucose regulation, insulin levels, and triglycerides.

This suggests that treatments targeting calorie intake and energy expenditure could potentially work together to produce stronger metabolic benefits.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär said.

In other words, the researchers do not necessarily envision TOFA replacing medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy. Instead, it could eventually become an additional treatment that helps address obesity and related metabolic conditions through a different biological mechanism.

A Promising Discovery, but Human Trials Are Still Needed.

In a recent development, despite the encouraging results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA remains an experimental compound. All the findings so far come from animal studies, and scientists have not yet established whether it is safe or effective in humans.

Further research will be necessary to determine whether the same metabolic improvements can be achieved in people and whether the treatment could offer meaningful advantages over existing medications.

Sources indicate that to help move the research toward potential clinical applications, the Berkeley scientists have established a biotechnology manufacturer called ReRx Therapeutics. The effort has received support from the university's life sciences entrepreneurship network, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck.

Recent findings suggest that if the findings eventually translate to humans, TOFA could represent an important addition to the growing range of treatments for obesity and diabetes. By encouraging the body to use more energy while helping preserve muscle, the compound points toward a potentially different way to achieve healthier weight loss.

The research was funded through discretionary resources provided by UC Berkeley, with additional support from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.

Industry observers note that additional authors include Chi Zhu, Melissa A. Boldridge, Rachelle L. Stark, Lei Xu, Federico Gonzalez, Xin Tang, Kaitlyn T. Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

There was a moment Ezra Frech didn’t have a leg to stand on—but he had a ballroom supporting him.

After the Paralympian’s prosthetic leg came off during his freestyle dance alongside partner Daniella Karagach on the Dancing With the Stars Nov. 24 finale, he revealed what went through his head before seamlessly reattaching the limb with the help of his partner as well as pro Alan Bersten.

It has been revealed that “The leg just wasn't on correctly, and I felt it,” he told Variety following the episode, which saw him and Karagach crowned as the season’s winners. “Sometimes it'll readjust and I'll be okay. And so, as I was running up the steps, I'm like, ‘There's a 50 percent chance my leg will resuction and I'll be okay.’ And that wasn't the case.”.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, he was ready to do what had to be done to finish the dance. After all, it was a moment he and Karagach had long been preparing for.

In a recent development, “I was just like, ‘Okay, I'm gonna do the rest of the dance on one leg. Like I'll do the entire thing on one leg,’” the 21-year-old continued. “She's drilled in me since the beginning that no matter what happens, we keep pushing through. You never give up, and you fight for it. And in this case, regardless of the circumstance, I was gonna do whatever I can to fight for it.”.

Thanks to the quick thinking of his pro, however, Frech was able to get a leg back up the competition—literally. During a brief pause in the dance, Karagach appeared to yell something to her partner as she handed him his prosthetic, allowing Frech a few beats to reattach the limb.

Sources indicate that “I heard her say, ‘Put your leg on,’” he recalled, “and I was like, ‘Yes, okay, yeah, good idea. I'll put it on right now.’”.

While Karagach had the utmost faith in her partner’s ability to persevere, she knew  taking the time to reattach the limb was worth it.

In a recent development, “I was just like, there is no other place in the routine that he can do this right now, and he cannot do the whole routine on one leg,” she explained. “So, I was like, ‘Just put your leg on.’ And it's not like—we had one little trick in there that he did on one, like a 540. It was really impressive. It was really great. But nothing's better than him just clicking on his leg properly and continuing on with the dance. I was like, ‘This is our only shot to do that.’”.

The moment was so adrenaline inducing, however, that Frech admitted he didn’t quite remember how his prosthetic made it back onto his body.

It has been revealed that “Did somebody give me the leg? Because I blacked out,” he asked aloud, to which Karagach confirmed she did. “You gave me the leg? Really?”.

Thankfully, those few seconds were the only thing Frech needed.

Sources indicate that “I clicked it on,” he said, “and when I put it on the second time. I was like, ‘Ooh it's on now, we're good.’”.

And good he was, with he and Karagach crowned the season 35 winners by the end of the episode—an accomplishment as good as gold for Frech.

"This is the most special moment of my life," he told the audience. "Thank you, everybody, for voting. Thank you for believing in us. Oh my God.".

City deny wronging and have appealed, but if the ruling is upheld, they could face an investigation by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).

It has the power to remove directors if they are deemed unsuitable, and even to force a sale of the club.

Appearing in front of parliament's Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee, IFR chairman David Kogan was clear that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate the club's hierarchy and take action, if deemed necessary.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the glitch. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," he said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so.

Sources indicate that "Would I, with an organisation that has a relatively new, fairly young staff, that's been going for less than a year, would I have chosen to have this particular problem in our laps this early? Well, probably not.

"But the truth is, if we don't act - assuming those circumstances are triggered - if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?

"So I think we have to absolutely, clearly be seen to be doing the job that you as legislators have asked us to do, and we absolutely will do that, whatever that means.".

#105052. Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite.
  • The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution.
  • It has been revealed that that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. Fresh research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.

The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.

It has been revealed that that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn.

Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.

However, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.

Each new fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.

Dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.

Sources indicate that "Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle said.

"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.

"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record.".

How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors.

To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.

The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

Industry observers note that A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.

Over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.

According to recent reports, an important concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.

Sources indicate that this approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.

Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans.

Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.

These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.

But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.

Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.

At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.

Sources indicate that together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.

Sources indicate that as a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.

A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution.

Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species right now classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.

In a recent development, the idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.

Recent findings suggest that such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever fresh fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.

In a recent development, the proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as new evidence has accumulated.

According to recent reports, "The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle noted.

"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups.".

Ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.

Latest Update: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
  • But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
  • That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.

But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.

That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

It has been revealed that "The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa stated ahead of the meeting.

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.

But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos noted in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Initiative.

However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on.".

Kos remarked that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.

For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.

Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

According to recent reports, bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.

From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.

North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.

EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova states North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.

It has been revealed that "We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.

After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

Recent findings suggest that A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.

That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.

The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.

The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.

For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.

The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.

According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

The Federal Aviation Administration mentioned Tuesday it would pause the installation of upcoming routers after problems with the technology led the agency to glitch a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

According to recent reports, tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have stated L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have mentioned they are working to figure out the root cause of the concern and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

Industry observers note that the senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Industry observers note that duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, remarked Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he noted. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

It has been revealed that duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and said it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prime Video's fresh "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov.
  • It has been revealed that this dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K.
  • Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Video's fresh "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

It has been revealed that this dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

According to recent reports, "When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over.".

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

In a recent development, "We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so fresh fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion.".

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey.".

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”.

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

Aaron Rodgers will be riding the bench.

“The Pittsburgh Steelers have named Mason Rudolph the starting quarterback for the game this Friday against the Denver Broncos,” Steelers spokesman Burt Lauten announced on Nov. 24. “Aaron Rodgers will be inactive for the game on Friday.”.

Recent findings suggest that for his part, Rodgers—who is not right now on the team’s injured reserve list—has not personally addressed the decision, and there have been no additional updates from the team, however he was not present at the start of the team's Nov. 25 practice.

The decision comes after the Steelers have lost their last two games, during which Rodgers only completed 45 of 73 passes, per ESPN, amounting to a completion rate of around 61 percent for this NFL season.

Yet, when asked about Rodgers’ future following the team’s loss against the Eagles on Nov. 22, head coach Mike McCarthy affirmed, “Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback.”.

For Rodgers, this season with Pittsburgh marks his last in the NFL, the 42-year-old having previously announced his prepares to retire after the 2026-2027 season, marking an end to more than two decades on the field.

As he told Pat McAfee in June, this final run with Pittsburgh “was really about finishing with a lot of love and fun and peace for the career that I've had.”.

According to recent reports, “I played 20 fricking years,” he added at the time. “It's been a long run. I've enjoyed it, and no better place to finish than in one of the cornerstone franchises of the NFL.”.

As for what inspired Rodgers to leave it all out on the field one last time, a conversation with his wife Brittani was the final push he needed. After all, he was already intrigued about hitching his wagon to the Pittsburgh team after McCarthy—under whom Rodgers played while on the Green Bay Packers—was named head coach.

"I thought last year might be it, and then Mike got hired,” Rodgers, who spent two seasons with the Fresh York Jets, told reporters during a July 28 press conference. "I talked to the wife. She said, 'You can do one more year and see if it works out.' And then it kind of all came together.".

Yet, no matter how this season plays out for the Steelers, whose record so far stands at 6-4, Rodgers will never again don an NFL helmet.

As he previously told reporters, there is “zero debate” about returning to the field after the 2026-2027 season: “This is it.”.

Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies.
  • The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted.
  • To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders.

Previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

Sources indicate that the University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

Sources indicate that "There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum noted.

Industry observers note that the team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

Industry observers note that however, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

In a recent development, "These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum remarked. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet.".

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases.

Recent findings suggest that before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several notable questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

Despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery.

For McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum said.

Recent findings suggest that mcCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

"It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he mentioned. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hexed is flying into cinemas like a teen witch wrangling her newfound magical powers. And if you're concentrating between chaotic cauldron chases, many-eyed monsters, and exploding potions, you'll spy a few Disney Easter eggs in the background.

Sources indicate that as Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) explores the magical realm of Hexe with her anxious mother Alice (Rashida Jones) and villainous Queen Celeste (Jodie Foster) on her heels, you might get caught up in all the spectacular sorcery. But if you keep your eyes peeled — all three in familiar Beef Roger Crummchuk's (Walton Goggins) case — you might spot a few references to Disney's animated film catalogue.

So, without spoiling the storyline, here's the Disney references directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand included in Hexed, with some easier to spot than others.

Early in the film (and seen in Hexed teasers), in Billie's room in Ohio, you can easily spot a rug that looks like Aladdin's magic carpet.

Also in Billie's room, on the back of her door, there's a sticker that resembles the Mad Hatter's top hat from Alice In Wonderland.

Painted blue with white crescents and stars, Billie's nail art could be a nod to the Disney sorcerer hat, first worn by Mickey Mouse in Fantasia. There's a related moment in the opening titles of the film, which sees Disney's Steamboat Willie Mickey animation transform into the Fantasia Mickey.

The Little Mermaid's glamorous bargain-maker finds a natural state of entrepreneurship in Hexe's town market, selling deals for "poor unfortunate souls" and showing off her previous customers in macabre jars of seawater.

But wait, this isn't Ursula. She's Cursula, and best of all, she's voiced by Jodi Benson, the icon behind Ariel in The Little Mermaid.

An overt Disney Easter egg that appeared in the trailer, you'll spot the enchanted dancing brooms from Fantasia doing their thing in the middle of the Haven Moon festival in the town square.

When Billie joins a magic class in the Haven Town square (also seen in the Hexed trailer), you can see a nearby tea shop with a sign showing one Mrs Potts from Beauty and the Beast, pouring tea into a teacup that's presumably her precious son, Chip.

When Billie first sees her mother arrive in Hexe (as seen in teasers) you can see a tall blue wizard hat, covered in crescent moons and stars, sitting at a stall. It could be another nod to the Disney sorcerer hat, however, it's accompanied by a long white beard, which suggests it actually belongs to the wizard Merlin from The Sword in the Stone.

Probably the hardest cameos to spot are those of voice actors, but one you might instantly recognise from other Disney films is Alan Tudyk, who plays the Enchanted Sign in Hexe's main town among others. You've heard Tudyk as Frozen's uptight Duke of Weselton, Moana fave Heihei, and Wreck-It Ralph's King Candy.

In a scene where Billie and Alice need to transform into animals, a towel emblazoned with The Little Mermaid's Ariel helps conceal their identities.

It's a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment, and I could be barking up the wrong tree here, but in a scene where Billie rapidly passes a group of farmers in a field, a boy lifts his hat to reveal a rat sitting atop his head. If that's not a reference to Ratatouille I'll eat this witch hat.

#105042. On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Navy rolled out the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.
  • Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.
  • Industry observers note that after World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy rolled out the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

Industry observers note that after World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were released.

It has been revealed that those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds.".

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful rolls out in the decades that followed.

According to recent reports, engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

#105040. Breaking: Now There’s a GLP-1 in Chocolate Form

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (708 w)
