Breaking: Now There’s a GLP-1 in Chocolate Form

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • First came GLP-1 injections, then GLP-1 pills.
  • According to recent reports, to be clear, this isn’t a new medication rubber-stamped by the Food and Drug Administration.
  • As GLP-1 shots exploded in popularity, Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, knew they could appeal to even more patients if they put their drugs in pill form.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First came GLP-1 injections, then GLP-1 pills. Now there’s GLP-1 chocolate. That’s right, a GLP-1 drug in chocolate.

According to recent reports, to be clear, this isn’t a new medication rubber-stamped by the Food and Drug Administration. It’s a copycat product offered by telehealth outfit Journi Health, and it’s aptly called Melt. The chocolate morsels, which are taken once daily, contain orforglipron, the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s prescription weight-loss pill Foundayo. (Eli Lilly also makes the GLP-1 injectable medications Mounjaro and Zepbound.).

As GLP-1 shots exploded in popularity, Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, knew they could appeal to even more patients if they put their drugs in pill form.

“One of the bigger barriers to adoption has been that some patients just don't want to take an injection,” Ken Custer, executive vice president of Eli Lilly, previously told WIRED. Foundayo was approved in April, while a pill version of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy won approval in December 2025.

Sources indicate that and here’s where Journi Health’s pitch comes in. Founder Luna Yu claims Melt is for people who have difficulty with injections or swallowing pills, including those who are newly introduced to GLP-1s as well as those already taking one who are looking to maintain their current weight. “Lastly, it's for the microdosers who are looking for the longevity benefits,” she says. (For the record, taking any GLP-1 medication below the lowest FDA-approved or standard therapeutic dose has not been tested or proven effective in human trials.).

Industry observers note that yu isn’t a doctor, but Melt does require a prescription from one. Would-be patients go through a virtual medical evaluation where a licensed clinician reviews their health history, determines if Melt is a good fit, and sets the dose. It costs $189 for a monthly subscription of 24 individually wrapped squares of chocolate, which includes physician review. (Foundayo’s list price is $649 for a 30-day supply, but with insurance it could be much lower.).

In a recent development, melt is considered a compounded drug, essentially a custom mix made for a patient by a pharmacy using FDA-approved ingredients but with a formulation that is not itself FDA approved. The FDA allows pharmacies to compound medications when there’s a patient need—for instance, if a patient is allergic to a dye or ingredient in a medication or needs a smaller dose because of their weight—or when the brand-name version is in shortage.

Industry observers note that when injectable GLP-1s were in shortage from 2022 through early 2025, compounding pharmacies were allowed to make their own versions for patients, leading to a booming online market. Telehealth companies sold their versions for a fraction of the price of the name-brand medications, making them a more affordable option for people without insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that commercial GLP-1s are no longer in shortage, the FDA claims pharmacies cannot routinely compound what are “essentially copies” en masse, though there are some exceptions for documented, patient-specific medical needs.

In a recent development, FDA has expressed particular concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs and has cracked down on virtual clinics selling them. Eli Lilly has filed multiple lawsuits against companies selling them, but the drugs still remain available online.

When asked about Journi’s Melt, a spokesperson for Eli Lilly told WIRED, “Foundayo is an FDA-approved oral orforglipron medicine, which was developed through years of innovative science and backed by robust clinical trials. An unstudied knockoff that uses chocolate for purported weight loss treats a serious health need as a marketing gimmick. Regulators and law enforcement must take decisive action against knockoff products being marketed to unsuspecting consumers.”.

Yu indicates Journi Health is able to offer Melt because it’s not an exact copy of the original. “It's really in a novel form factor whereby it allows the patient to have a different experience.” Plus, she says, an edible formulation meets a need for patients who have trouble with injections or swallowing pills.

“We've spoken with patients who've discontinued treatment because of these barriers,” she says. “They deserve alternatives worth exploring.”.

Whether the FDA will find this convincing remains to be determined. For now, though, all that stands between patients and the “novel form factor” is a few clicks.

#105039. CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1460 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • Industry observers note that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played vital roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

Industry observers note that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

Sources indicate that it also creates newly introduced opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal Latest Physics.

According to recent reports, the LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

According to recent reports, when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Sources indicate that particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

Recent findings suggest that according to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

Industry observers note that "The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering latest technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

In a recent development, one of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

Recent findings suggest that "We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

Industry observers note that this name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

In a recent development, "There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

According to recent reports, "The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

Sources indicate that the upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

Researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to notable advances in understanding nature.

"This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful fresh way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

Tech Report: Should Sunrise on the Reaping be the last Hunger Games movie?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that over its opening weekend, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping topped the domestic box office with an impressive $120 million, making it just one of five movies to open with over $100 million this year.
  • Industry observers note that with Sunrise on the Reaping's massive success comes questions about the future of the franchise.
  • It has been revealed that alternatively, what if we just let the franchise rest for a little longer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hunger Games has never been more back.

Recent findings suggest that over its opening weekend, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping topped the domestic box office with an impressive $120 million, making it just one of five movies to open with over $100 million this year. Other titles to achieve that goal are Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day, Toy Story 5, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, and The Odyssey.

Industry observers note that with Sunrise on the Reaping's massive success comes questions about the future of the franchise. What could our next trip to Panem look like? Which character could author Suzanne Collins focus on in a latest novel? Oft-floated options include fan-favorite victor Finnick Odair (Sam Claflin), which would give audiences a look at a Career's experience in the Hunger Games, or Gamemaker Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), which would offer a different perspective on the rebellion against President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

It has been revealed that alternatively, what if we just let the franchise rest for a little longer? That seems to be the plan for now, as Lionsgate chairman Adam Fogelson told Variety that there would be no more newly introduced films until Collins wrote another book. And honestly, if Collins chooses to move on from Panem forever, would that be so awful? The Hunger Games has proven it has staying power, but with Sunrise on the Reaping, it's also begun to show the limits of the books' formula. Not that Sunrise on the Reaping is bad — far from it! However, it does make a pretty solid case as to why it should be the franchise's closer.

When Collins first confirmed the release of Sunrise on the Reaping, I was skeptical. Film audiences already knew how Haymitch Abernathy's (Joseph Zada) games would end. Book readers had even seen it play out in an abridged version on the page in Catching Fire, when Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) watched it to prepare for the Third Quarter Quell.

Still, Collins proved me wrong. The novel deepened our understanding of the Capitol's propaganda machine, revealing that the version of Haymitch's games that Katniss and Peeta watched was edited to omit Haymitch's attempt to break the arena. It also emphasized that characters from the original trilogy like Haymitch, Plutarch, Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke) had all been working to undermine Snow since before Katniss was even born. Yes, their sparks of rebellion didn't catch fire at first. But we know that they eventually build and build until Snow is overthrown in Mockingjay. By the end of the book, Haymitch lives to see the sun rise on his birthday with no reaping in site, adding a bittersweet layer to the hard-fought tragedy of his games.

Industry observers note that sunrise on the Reaping, both the film and the novel, closes with the return of Katniss and Peeta, now grown up. Their appearance brings Sunrise on the Reaping full circle, looking to Panem's future while also deepening our understanding of its past. Do we really need to break that circle open again when Collins has already written such a meaningful conclusion?

In a recent development, my biggest complaint about the book and film versions of Sunrise on the Reaping is the same: They both suffer from prequel-itis. That's when a prequel is so focused on linking back to the original title that it becomes bogged down in references and callbacks. In Sunrise on the Reaping's case, that prequel-itis manifests in the nonstop barrage of returning characters, whose presence can almost suffocate the new characters. Collins still weaves a compelling story of rebellion with them, but by the time young Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning) showed up, I almost rolled my eyes at how connected everything was.

Recent findings suggest that if Collins returns to Panem to tell the story of a known character like Finnick or Plutarch, it's possible that novel would suffer a similar fate. The world of the series would grow ever smaller, instead of expanding. Collins could also opt to avoid the Hunger Games entirely and focus instead on the Dark Days before the Capitol created the Games. But without the spectacle of the Hunger Games themselves, how can Lionsgate expect audiences to show up? After all, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes only featured a rudimentary version of the Hunger Games, and it took in $44 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend, a little over a third of Sunrise on the Reaping's total. The disparity proves that people want to see the Hunger Games on a large scale, preferably with familiar faces. But when it comes to storytelling, those desires might wind up being greater flaws than boons in the long run.

Again, Collins proved my skepticism about Sunrise on the Reaping dead wrong, and I'd like to think that she truly won't write another Hunger Games novel unless she has something new and compelling to say. But given that Sunrise on the Reaping serves as such a fitting bookend to the original trilogy, and that it's beginning to show the warning signs of franchise fatigue, it might be best to let it stand as a strong conclusion, as opposed to a gateway for further meddling in a well-trodden story.

US tech company Nvidia noted on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO "effective immediately.".

This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia stated, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead.".

Meanwhile, the 63-year-old said in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the tech giant and that he would take on the renewed responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.".

He thanked interim CEO Colette Kress, who is set to return to her role as chief financial officer.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang stated. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work.".

US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure.".

"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, also saying that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct.

Huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed.

The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York.

The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170.

#105033. A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate?
  • In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr.
  • The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, newly introduced research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

"The claim that mutation is slower for key genes is a triumph of hype over substance," said Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the new paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.".

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution.

It has been revealed that the conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

However, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

Sources indicate that at first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

According to recent reports, the problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations.

It has been revealed that another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Vital genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are swiftly eliminated from populations.

Professor Hurst said: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more important genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'.".

This distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory.

To investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

The scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Industry observers note that dr. Radrizzani said: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date.".

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more crucial for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

In a recent development, they assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

According to recent reports, if the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Professor Hurst mentioned: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate.".

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

Industry observers note that the team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more important genes receive special protection.

Dr. Radrizzani remarked: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate.".

Recent findings suggest that that does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Industry observers note that professor Hurst mentioned: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm.".

The research therefore provides newly introduced support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most important genes by reducing how often they mutate.

It’s one of the most beloved pop songs of the past 15 years — but never one of its biggest chart hits. Carly Rae Jepsen‘s “Run Away With Me” became a cult classic almost immediately upon its single release (from her enduring E•MO•TION album) in 2015, but Billboard Hot 100 success totally eluded it in its moment. (In 2023, Billboard named it the 21st greatest pop song of the Hot 100 era to never reach the chart.) But in 2026, a great pop song still has a chance to reach the Hot 100 no matter when it was originally released — and “Run Away With Me” now has the best opportunity it’s had in a decade, thanks to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Sources indicate that “Run Away With Me” plays in the record-breaking latest game during a scene when its dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, are enjoying the Vice City high life after the latter’s release from prison. With its cinematic sax and propulsive synth-pop shuffle making it an ideal soundtrack for just about any action-packed sequence, the song has become one of the breakout musical moments from the game’s heavily music-focused universe — and led many pop fans to wonder if it could result in the storied track finally reaching the Hot 100 for the first time.

The answer? Maybe — but it still has a long way to go.

The song’s streaming breakout has unquestionably been real: It was pulling daily official on-demand streams in the low 20,000s in the days before the game’s release, but that number had broken six digits by Sunday (Nov. 22, three days after GTA VI‘s release), and was all the way up to 281,000 by Monday, according to early data provided by Luminate. That’s a gain of nearly 1,100% over the total the song posted last Wednesday, just before the game’s release, but it’s still a little low for a streaming-driven-song on the Hot 100.

It has been revealed that the question is if the song can continue its viral growth throughout this week, and maybe even into next week. It’s got a bit of a late start for this tracking week, which runs through Thursday — and as of Tuesday, the song still wasn’t streaming enough to enter the daily top 200 on either Spotify or Apple Music — so its best chance of breaching the chart might come next week, especially if it continues to grow and then stays stable, with daily U.S. streaming numbers more in the 500k-600k range.

However, it will be getting late early on the charts for songs like “Run Away With Me” by next week — since the yearly avalanche of Christmas-related titles, which has already provided a pretty heavy snowfall on the Hot 100 in November, will really hit following Thanksgiving. At that point, non-holiday-related space on the chart will become increasingly limited, and the bar that “Run” needs to clear in order to reach the listing will climb higher and higher.

It has been revealed that it will be a challenge for “Run Away With Me” to broach the Hot 100 — but it definitely could happen, if its moment continues to spread and attract newly introduced fans while re-activating old ones. Could it get extra momentum through new TikTok trends? Will a still-unreleased remix from Overmono — featured in the game, but not yet available on streaming — end up as an crucial wildcard? Might pop radio belateedly decide to embrace it, in a way it never quite did a decade ago? Could its best chance of breaking the chart not actually come next week, but next year?

In a recent development, it’s too early to say on any of this, but one thing is for sure: Its longtime fans will be there rooting it on, supporting as much as they can and air-saxing the whole way. — ANDREW UNTERBERGER.

Recent findings suggest that outside of Morgan Wallen’s “Last Thing You Need,” the all-star jam “Flower in a Hurricane” was already the closest thing to a pre-minted hit from the Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album soundtrack, having already spent multiple weeks on the Hot 100. But following the game’s release, the song from Justice, Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard has reached a newly introduced level of popularity — and may soon challenge or even eclipse even the commercially bulletproof Wallen’s latest hit single on the Hot 100.

In the four days following the game’s Nov. 19 release, “Flower’ racked up nearly 7.6 million official on-demand U.S. streams, according to early data provided by Luminate — a 165% gain over the 2.9 million streams the songs racked up over the previous Friday-Monday period (Nov. 13-16). While doing so, it also topped Spotify’s Daily Top Songs USA chart and reached No. 3 on the Apple Music realtime chart. It all portends another huge jump for “Flower” on next week week’s Hot 100, with the song already reaching a new peak of No. 45 this week, and looking to shoot into the top 20 or possibly even the top 10 next week.

But that’s not all for Justice — the French house duo also responsible for composing the game’s epic score — who has two additional fresh original collabs on the game’s official soundtrack. One of those, the album-opening “Starting From Zero” — a teamup with yacht rock icon Michael McDonald — is also off to a strong start on streaming, earning 1.8 million streams in its first four days of release (Nov. 20-23), and potentially pushing for an outside chance at a Hot 100 debut of its own if its numbers keep climbing. (The duo’s third GTA song, “Pusher” with Gesaffelstein, is also up 53% to 464,000 streams.).

And Wallen’s “Last Thing”? That’s up about 31% too over that four-day period — albeit with a lower streaming total now (around 6 million) than “Hurricane” — and should also be due for a chart rebound from its current No. 17 perch, possibly back to the chart’s top 10. — AU.

Recent findings suggest that after The Cars‘ “Drive” reached No. 3 on the Hot 100 during its initial 1984 run, the dramatic rock classic is back in the cultural mainstream following its key sync in the newly released Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

In a recent development, in the Friday-Monday period (Nov. 13-16) preceding the game’s Nov. 19 release, “Drive” collected 629,000 official on-demand U.S. streams. In the Friday-Monday period following the game’s release (Nov. 20-23), that total leapt 83% to over 1.15 million official on-demand U.S. streams, according to early data provided by Luminate.

Even though Rockstar Games teamed up with Atlantic Records for a gargantuan, genre-spanning, 57-song compilation soundtrack, “Drive” remained the developers’ North Star. Billboard’s latest cover story revealed that Rockstar first tried to clear “Drive” for GTA in 2002, but this year’s long-awaited sync “was a testament to the company’s unwavering prioritization of music, the relationships it has cultivated throughout the industry and the meticulous curation that has transformed Grand Theft Auto into one of the past 20 years’ most culture-saturating, riveting and lucrative products.” With first-day sales of $3.79 billion, “Drive” now soundtracks one of the biggest monocultural moments of the decade — and indeed, is the first song players hear play on the in-game radio.

Industry observers note that “Drive” also experienced a smaller resurgence in 2019, following the death of frontman Ric Ocasek. The song returned to No. 6 on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs back then, and to No. 27 on Digital Song Sales. – KYLE DENIS.

Despite being born in the 1970s, Stephen Wilson Jr. was named country music’s fresh artist of the year at the Country Music Awards last Wednesday (Nov. 18) — capping an incredible journey that’s taking Wilson from the science lab at Mars Inc. to songwriting rooms in Nashville, to now his own success as a solo singer-songwriter. The 47-year-old singer-songwriter was one of the biggest non-Ella Langley presences at the ceremonies, not only winning new artist of the year and giving a memorably emotional speech following the win, but also performing his new single “I’m a Song” alongside fellow country powerhouse (and 2026 CMA Award winner) Chris Stapleton.

Industry observers note that and it seems like the awards might only be the beginning of Wilson’s mainstream breakthrough, as his streaming numbers shot through the roof following his big night. His catalog drew 8.7 million official on-demand U.S. streams over the three days following the awards (Nov. 19-21), more than tripling the under 2.9 million streams he amassed over the prior Thursday-Saturday period. The biggest gains from that period were of course reserved for “I’m a Song” (up a staggering 1,089% to 1.4 million streams), as well as his breakout cover of Ben E. King’s “Stand By Me” (up 135% to 1.1 million) and his CMA Award-nominated 2026 single “Gary” (up 281% to 753,000).

Industry observers note that and of course, Ella Langley also saw a bump from her five wins — including for her big winners, record-breaking Hot 100 smash “Choosin’ Texas” (up 11% to 8.6 million streams) and Billboard 200-topping album Dandelion (up 16% to 24.2 million), as well as for her acoustically performed “Loving Life Again” (up 17% to 2.5 million). – AU.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mix of elements that ends up in planets — even people — can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star, latest space observations suggest.

According to recent reports, A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A, a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star. Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, the astronomers could parse out clumps within the 350-year-old cloud and analyze their compositions. The debris from the explosion, called a supernova, is still racing outward in space at about 11 million mph.

"What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," said Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement.

It has been revealed that supernova explosions forge and scatter many of the heavy elements that later get recycled into latest stars and worlds. Computer models have long predicted that a star's inner layers could merge before it explodes. But scientists don't fully understand why and how some stars go through this violent process. The new study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds evidence that it happened in Cassiopeia A, giving astronomers a way to peer inside a star that hasn't existed for centuries.

Recent findings suggest that A massive star builds up in layers, like an onion, with each shell fusing a different element. When the star explodes, some of that material cools into dust. Each layer makes its own kind of dust, so the grains, smaller than the width of a human hair, keep a record of what sat where inside the star.

As the layers merge, they can change the mix of elements the blast flings out, said Tea Temim, lead author of the study.

Sources indicate that "So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly," noted Temim, a research scientist at Columbia University in Fresh York. "And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion.".

To look for evidence, the team pointed Webb at three spots in Cassiopeia A, or Cas A, that NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope had previously flagged. Spitzer saw the debris as a blur, with light from many clumps mixed together. Webb's sharper view separates individual clumps, each roughly the size of our solar system, so the team could study them one at a time.

Recent findings suggest that one clump held mostly silica dust, the main ingredient in most sand. Another held mostly carbon dust. The third sits in a feature nicknamed the Green Monster, and its dust is rich in magnesium and silicon. That material didn't come from the blast at all; rather, the star shed it before it exploded.

In a recent development, the researchers then compared their measurements with existing computer models of exploding stars. Only the models in which the star's layers had merged could reproduce both the silica-rich and the carbon-rich debris. A wider Webb dust map highlights signs of the merger across much of the cloud.

Sources indicate that the team cautions that those models are incomplete. Researchers will need more detailed 3D simulations — and Webb observations of more spots in the cloud — to confirm the merger.

This approach also could help astronomers make sense of supernovas in other galaxies.

"I think it's remarkable that we can watch these changes and understand what they mean from thousands of light-years away," Milisavljevic remarked.

SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

In a recent development, A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously rolled out NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force releases (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions introduced by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

Booking Holdings is bringing together two of its business-to-business travel operations in a upcoming division it hopes will be transformational, betting that a larger, coordinated partner platform can generate growth as artificial intelligence changes how travelers discover and book trips.

According to recent reports, the new enterprise unit, dubbed Booking Partner Division, will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships with Rocket Travel by Agoda, and is set to begin operating in January. Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern will lead the unit, which aims to help businesses such as banks, airlines and online travel companies sell trips or build branded experiences for their customers.

"We realize that if we focus our efforts both on the product side, but also on the go-to-market side, then we can potentially grow faster and serve better partners," Morgenshtern told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

He said existing partners will find upcoming and better products, which will also help grow the partner base.

According to recent reports, the move gives Booking a single organization to coordinate technology, travel supply and commercial expertise across business relationships. The company notes partners will be able to use its global supply and technology through white-label platforms, integrated applications, branded solutions and hotel-chain rate distribution.

The portfolio includes more than 4.7 million properties, 33 million accommodation listings, more than 500 airlines and more than 200 car rental providers, according to the company.

Competitor Expedia Group has seen notable growth by prioritizing its enterprise efforts, including a strategy rolled out in 2022 to make its technology platform available to business partners looking to add travel to their own offerings.

From 2018 to 2023, Expedia’s business-to-business revenue grew at a 16% compound annual rate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, for the division grew at a 28% rate, the manufacturer said in 2024.

According to recent reports, in 2025, Expedia’s B2B revenue rose 18% to $4.8 billion, and its segment adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to $1.26 billion. Those figures represented about a third of Expedia’s total revenue and more than a third of its adjusted EBITDA for the full year.

Morgenshtern declined to say how much the upcoming division is expected to contribute to Booking Holdings' overall revenue and profit, but he said the opportunity for growth is immense, estimating the total addressable market at $2 trillion.

Online travel agencies have been pressured this year as investors scrutinize how AI will change the way customers search for and then book their travel.

Companies that offer lodging, experiences and other travel and leisure are grappling with how to stay visible if AI tools become the new starting point for planning and reservations.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro noted on the organization’s earnings call Tuesday that guests already use AI to discover and proposal Disney trips, and that some are using the tools to book.

“Ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools,” he mentioned, adding that Disney is exploring ways to let guests make reservations directly from them.

Booking anticipates offering partners AI capabilities that draw on the company's existing travel know-how while minimizing token costs, it noted.

"I see a lot of AI demos," Morgenshtern said, drawing a distinction between a product that caters to a few customers and one that's scalable and works even when overloaded by travel emergencies. He said he's "super optimistic" about the bespoke product — a vertical agent — that Booking will offer to its partners.

Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," states Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. Fresh research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," states Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

Members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

These contrasting perspectives may have important consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to new evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

It has been revealed that dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

According to recent reports, the researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

In a recent development, some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as latest challenges arise.

Sources indicate that dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

According to recent reports, another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

Sources indicate that one possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

Sources indicate that the differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when new evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

With researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

In a recent development, the study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

In a recent development, "Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she says. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

Tech Report: ‘GTA 6’ Is a Birder’s Paradise

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI has received near-universal acclaim and could be the highest-grossing entertainment launch in history.
  • According to recent reports, rockstar Games has filled the latest GTA installation with over 170 animal species that players can tally in their logbook.
  • Sources indicate that I myself am not a gamer, but I’m an avid birder based in Latest York City who’s familiar with a few indie birdwatching games like Alba and Flock Around, and I have done a bit of birding in Florida—which GTA VI is modeled after, with Vice City being a stand-in for Miami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI has received near-universal acclaim and could be the highest-grossing entertainment launch in history. But it holds a more esoteric honor: It might be the most accurately rendered depiction of Florida’s bird life to appear in a video game.

According to recent reports, rockstar Games has filled the latest GTA installation with over 170 animal species that players can tally in their logbook. At the same time, there’s been an explosion of interest in birdwatching, especially among young people, since the last GTA came out 13 years ago. While many players have gotten busy stealing jets and going to strip clubs, birders and streamers are doing “ornithologist runs” to see as many bird species as they can.

Sources indicate that I myself am not a gamer, but I’m an avid birder based in Latest York City who’s familiar with a few indie birdwatching games like Alba and Flock Around, and I have done a bit of birding in Florida—which GTA VI is modeled after, with Vice City being a stand-in for Miami. So I was hungry to get my hands on GTA VI and see the birds for myself. Were the details of GTA VI’s avian NPCs as lifelike as its human ones? (Full disclosure that a friend of mine worked on the game, though not the birds specifically.).

You receive a pair of binoculars with the first mission, and most of the map is open to explore once the intro is over, so you can begin your birding adventures immediately. I left the house and walked around town, trying to get a sense of the neighborhood and searching for places I knew I’d find wildlife, as I would in real life. It turns out you don’t have to look hard. Birds are everywhere in GTA VI—brown pelicans soared overhead, a flock of house sparrows alighted onto a telephone wire, and a blue jay stared down at me as I rounded a corner.

I zeroed in on a gull perched atop a building and noticed its partial black hood of feathers, an adult laughing gull. In a sign of how committed Rockstar is to accurately portraying the real world, I walked further and noticed a bird with the same shape, but it was grayer and light on the black feathers, an immature laughing gull.

Recent findings suggest that this is GTA VI, and all means of improving your birding experience are at your disposal—legal or not. With that in mind, I headed toward the water and performed my first act of theft, jacking a kayak so I could inspect the mangroves and sandy islands in the bay. While motorboats were available, I opted for human-powered to avoid scaring the birds.

In a recent development, the sky was filled with iconic South Florida birds like white ibises, magnificent frigate birds, and osprey. I shouted excitedly on spotting a flock of Caspian terns loafing on a small islet’s shore, then eyed a spotted sandpiper. The latter didn’t have its real-world analogue’s “twerking” strut (a big missed opportunity for a GTA game), but its physical appearance was accurate. I beached my kayak and went ashore, where I eyed a pair of great blue herons and then scared a tricolored heron from a shrub as I sprinted away from a crocodile I nearly stepped on.

Industry observers note that I was impressed by the game developer’s commitment to accurately rendering South Florida’s coastal mangrove habitats, which provide shelter for an abundance of fish, food for birds, and serve as a habitat for the threatened American crocodile. However, they only host so much avian diversity.

Sources indicate that to see more species, I drove north through the various habitats in and around the fictional city of Leonida and stopped to scan the skies. I spotted American robins, northern mockingbirds, and “Newly introduced World orioles,” the game’s analog to the Baltimore oriole, which I assumed is named as such because Baltimore is not part of the Grand Theft Auto universe. Downtown Vice City featured non-native peacocks and rock pigeons—the latter of which were introduced to North America in the 1600s. When I arrived at the pine-covered areas north of the city, I began seeing red-cockaded woodpeckers and scrub jays, an analog to the rare Florida scrub-jay that similarly inhabits sand pine areas north of Miami and is endemic to the state of Florida.

Recent findings suggest that birders who’ve been to Florida will find Leonida’s abundance and distribution of wildlife familiar. As in meatspace, pelicans and ibises are constantly flying overhead, and wading birds fill every body of water. Birds are properly segregated into their habitats, with songbirds and city birds in built-up areas, shorebirds and long-legged wading birds in wetlands. In both the game and real life, despite intensive human development, birds still attempt to survive where they can.

In a recent development, the birds’ behaviors are also accurate beyond standing and flying. As I was trying to study my first bald eagle, a pair of crows flew over to chase it, a behavior regularly seen in the wild to scare large raptors away. Monk parakeets preened while perching on a wire, and a juvenile northern mockingbird did its characteristic wing flicking. Meanwhile, GTA VI’s great blue herons always seem to be having sex, not something I’ve noticed in real life but a silly detail nonetheless.

Frankly, the whole experience of driving around while distractedly watching telephone wires and roadsides or pulling over to check every little water body is itself the most accurate representation of the Florida birding experience.

My other birding friends who have played the game concurred. “The first thing I thought was how closely this resembles birding in Florida,” claims accomplished bird author Nick Lund, who has done extensive birdwatching in Red Dead Redemption II, another game where avian life is a big part of gameplay, and is currently doing a GTA VI birding speed run. He’s noticed other in-game birding Easter eggs—for example, he’s encountered spot-breasted orioles, a Central American species introduced to southeastern Florida that birdwatchers specifically target when visiting Miami.

It has been revealed that while impressive in its fidelity to real life, GTA VI’s avian depictions aren’t 100 percent accurate. I found the flight styles and silhouettes of many birds to be a little off, while some renditions missed the mark—the abundant crows all feel too long and pale. While walking around Jason’s neighborhood, Lund and I both noticed the apparent song of the bananaquit, a Caribbean species that rarely appears in the US. The game is also filled with whooping cranes, one of the rarest birds in the US. They’re also mostly gone from Florida after an unsuccessful reintroduction effort, where sandhill cranes are much more common. (Maybe the makers of GTA VI are telling real-world conservationists to try harder next time.) Lund flagged that the roseate spoonbill seems to make the call of the willow ptarmigan—a detail he also noticed in RDR II. And somehow I’ve yet to spot a bird in a tree, but this may be a skill glitch.

Ultimately, GTA VI isn’t a birdwatching game, and does lag behind the real world and birdwatching-specific games in terms of avian content. Sixty-two species might sound like a lot, but birders in Miami-Dade County have spotted more than 240 species in November 2026 alone, and one real-life birder in Miami spotted 61 species in a two-hour stint on the day of the game’s release.

There’s a certain magic and unpredictability to birdwatching that the game doesn’t nail—finding a migratory warbler in a hotel parking lot, catching an egret hunting anoles in a topiary, or spotting an out-of-place vagrant bird are all real-life thrills the game can’t fully capture. Of course, GTA VI also has an actual plot and storyline that I surmise might be slightly more notable to its developers and the majority of the gaming public than solely building the world’s most accurate Florida birding simulator.

Sources indicate that still, GTA VI’s animal observation mechanics have continued to delight after 12 hours of play. Birding is certainly an auxiliary part of the game, rather than its core thrust—but if you’re a birder wondering whether to play the game just for its birds, I think you’ll still have plenty of fun.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Luke-ing” back across the years, Luke Bryan didn’t have much country competition in branding his name.

Hank Williams recorded a series of recitations under the pseudonym Luke the Drifter, and stretching the boundaries a bit, Waylon Jennings had a landmark hit with “Luckenbach, Texas (Back to the Basics of Love).” Bryan got used to being known in the genre by a single syllable until a “Hurricane” hit in 2016.

It has been revealed that “I thought I had the Luke name,” Bryan states. “I thought I had that solidly before Luke Combs. I mean, the disc jockeys could just say, ‘That was Luke.’ They didn’t have to verify last names.” Related Dolly Parton to Receive CNN Heroes Legacy Award, Miley Cyrus to Accept on Her Behalf ESSENCE Festival of Culture Moving On From New Orleans After Three Decades: 'Memories Were Made -- And So Was History' Noah Kahan Caps Epic Year With 'Live From the Great Divide' Album Explore Luke Bryan Luke Combs See latest videos, charts and news.

See latest videos, charts and news.

It has been revealed that not that Bryan has a problem with the situation. In fact, he enlisted Combs as a feature voice on “Finders Keepers,” released by Row Crop/MCA Nashville to country radio via PlayMPE on Oct. 12. It lists on Billboard’s Country Airplay as “Luke Bryan & Luke Combs,” though Bryan doesn’t particularly care how people refer to them.

“Luke Squared,” he indicates, “whatever you want to call it.”.

According to recent reports, the song’s writers were just happy they got the call. Bryan heard it — and recorded it — 15 days after its official date of creation when his manager, KP Entertainment founder/president Kerri Edwards, was going through unopened emails during Bryan’s session at Nashville’s Ocean Way on March 6. She played it for Bryan and his producers, Jeff and Jody Stevens, during their drive to Dicey’s Tavern on a lunch break, and they added it to that afternoon’s material. The musicians picked it up easily.

“They ran through it one time, and ran through it another time, and that was it,” Jeff recalls.

Songwriter Sam Ellis (“What If I Never Get Over You,” “More Hearts Than Mine”) hosted the writing session that spawned “Finders Keepers” on Feb. 19 at his East Nashville studio. When the initial song ideas fell flat for Ellis and his co-writers, Jimi Bell (“Backup Proposal,” “Last Night Lonely”) and Beau Bailey (“Stay Country or Die Tryin’,” “Favorite Country Song”), Bailey apologetically mentioned a hook he’d concocted during a brainstorming exercise: “Finders keepers, losers drinkers.” No apology was necessary; his co-writers loved the wordplay.

“They just went to town,” Bailey indicates, “They’re lyrical and musical assassins.”.

They had chatted up their passion for Dwight Yoakam at the start of the appointment, and they used the pace of Yoakam’s “Suspicious Minds” cover, from the 1992 Honeymoon in Vegas soundtrack, as a template for “Finders Keepers.”.

“I’m a huge Dwight Yoakam fan, so that was 100% channeled that day,” Bell says. “As soon as he said that title, I kind of heard a Dwight Yoakam thing in my mind.”.

In a recent development, they sketched out the musical framework for it, ensuring that the chorus would start in an energetic place. It was obvious that the plot needed to address a broken heart, and the song’s second line, “Made a home in that hole you dug,” acknowledged the protagonist blew it. “You do know it’s his fault,” Ellis claims, “and you’re kind of on his side.”.

They doubled down on the breakup a few lines later with “She took the ‘U’ right out of ‘us,’” though the twist in that phrase may escape most listeners until they see the lyrics in print.

In a recent development, “It’s always fun when you can sneak a little bit of smartness into a happy, full-on, go-lucky drinking song,” Bailey notes. “Then when you dissect it, you’re like, ‘Wait, this actually makes sense. We haven’t heard it said like this.’”.

They introduced the “Finders keepers, losers drinkers” hook in amped-up fashion to start the chorus, though returning to that hook for the payoff presented a challenge. Those four words worked better as a set up for the last line, which ultimately became a consolation prize for the guy on his barstool: “Hey man, at least the beer is cold.”.

The chorus ended that way for a bit, but as they worked with it further, it called out for more. So they tacked a post-chorus line onto the cold beer: “So grab you one, the night is good, and the night is young.” That phrase came with three-part harmony, performed mostly over a heavy kick drum, a la Alabama’s “Mountain Music.” The second time around, the post-chorus grew even longer, as the Alabama section focused on the hot girls dancing: “Don’t look now, one’s lookin’ your way.”.

“I love just having those dualities,” Bell says, “turning what otherwise would have been a kind of a sad situation into a party song.”.

Sources indicate that bell sang lead for the demo, produced by Ellis with an instrumental break featuring an electric guitar that handed off the back half of the solo to a steel guitar. They thought the song was a winner — that Alabama-styled post-chorus cinched it — and Bell’s publisher, Worktape Music owner/operator Travis Gordon, envisioned it for Bryan. When Edwards played it for her artist, Bryan was won over by the Alabama sound. “It’s kind of a little cherry on top at the end of the chorus,” he states.

Returning from lunch, Bryan’s creative team made some small changes to the demo’s arrangement, particularly for the final chorus, where Jeff Stevens reworked the chord structure. “They had gone to a chord progression that, to me, didn’t feel like it contributed to the energy level that it should be at that point in the song,” he claims.

They went back to the original chords and had drummer Miles McPherson — working his first Bryan session — deaden cymbal crashes with his hands to create a power sound. They brought fiddler Joe Spivey into Sound Emporium to enhance the old-school country sound, though Spivey was hesitant to play anything outside of long notes, since the original band had already filled up much of the space.

Recent findings suggest that “It just felt like it was slowing it down,” Jody indicates. “It needed some fiddle parts that moved with the rhythm of the song.”.

Sources indicate that jody dictated some simmering passages, and Spivey nailed it within 10 minutes. Bryan’s tracking-day vocals weren’t where he wanted them — “I had come off the road,” he claims, “and I sounded like a coyote caught in a bear trap” — but he knocked out the final version in a date at Blackbird Studios.

In a recent development, next up, background vocalist Trey Keller mirrored the demo’s original harmonies, but Jeff had him redo the part, creating more of a Ricky Skaggs bluegrass tone. All of those pieces were in place when Bryan sent “Finders Keepers” to Combs, who agreed immediately to sing on it. Jeff and Jody recorded him at producer-engineer Chip Matthews’ studio in three short takes.

“We couldn’t have been in there more than about 30 minutes for vocals,” Jody claims.

Sources indicate that edwards later played it for Bell and Ellis in person, and they flipped out when they heard Combs emerge on verse two — they’d not projected it as a collaboration. The Luke Squared dueling voices made it a likely radio release, but Ellis also hoped to hear it outside the bars on Nashville’s Lower Broadway.

“I wanted this thing to sound like downtown, where you’re walking by and you can hear a band in the distance playing it,” he notes. “That’s something you want to hear cruising down Broadway, you know, chicken picking and all that stuff.”.

Industry observers note that it’s working well on radio, positioned at No. 30 on the Country Airplay chart dated Nov. 28. And Bryan is focused on its concert benefits, too.

“I’m really in an uptempo mood these days,” he notes. “I want to put songs out that could go right into the set list for my tours and really add a lot of energy.”.

Gukesh to defend chess crown against rising star Sindarov

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.
  • "I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.

"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he said.

Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.

It has been revealed that gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He currently languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.

Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.

"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov stated.

Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.

Sources indicate that "He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.

"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot.".

By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.

"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.

"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift.".

While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.

Now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.

"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson mentioned.

It has been revealed that another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad.".

Additional reporting by: Thomas Lemmer.

#105020. Breaking: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)
