💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.
  • NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept.
  • Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.

NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept. 26, 2022, when it slammed into Dimorphos, the small moonlet of the much larger asteroid Didymos. The mission tested if such an impact could be deployed to divert an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Scientists have known for some time that this deflection attempt was successful; the system's orbit around the sun was lengthened by 33 minutes, but the European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera mission released in October 2024 to travel the 120 million miles (194 million kilometers) to the Didymos system to observe the effect of the DART impact in greater detail.

Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically. The impact also appears to have blasted out hundreds of previously unknown boulders that are now circling the binary asteroids.

"Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same," Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, mentioned in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that "Much to our surprise, the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width.".

Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, detailed some of the changes to the impacted moonlet seen by the spacecraft: "As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit.

"Another major surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size.".

It wasn't all change for Dimorphos. Hera discovered that the boulder fields covering the regions of the moonlet not impacted look just like they did when DART imaged it in 2022.

Hera isn't finished with Didymos and its moonlet. The ESA spacecraft is currently in a rectangular orbit around the asteroid binary system, using its thrusters to maintain a distance of around 18.6 miles (30 kilometers). This allows Hera to continue observing Didymos and Dimorphos.

In a recent development, hera will soon come to within around 8 miles (13 km) of the asteroids, capturing even more detailed images of the space rocks. Following this, it will deploy two showbox-sized CubeSats, which will get even closer to the asteroids.

In a recent development, the CubeSat Juventas will use low-frequency radar to probe the interior of Dimorphos, the first time this has ever been done for an asteroid, and will eventually attempt to land on the moonlet to measure its gravity. Meanwhile, the Milani CubeSat will prospect asteroid materials and dust around the Didymos system.

Together, Hera and its CubeSats will more precisely determine the mass of Dimorphos, which, when combined with information about the orbital change of the system, will be crucial in planning missions to deflect threatening asteroids.

Hera's observations were revealed on Wednesday (Nov. 25) at the dinosaur hall of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, Germany. That location isn't a coincidence: It is a stark reminder of why this planetary defense mission is so notable. Especially if humanity doesn't want to go the way of the dinosaurs, whose rule on Earth ended when an asteroid fell from the sky."Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth. Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli explained. "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. "By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.".

#104957. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)

A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • Recent findings suggest that new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

Recent findings suggest that new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

It has been revealed that despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising fresh questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

In a recent development, "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred states. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

The researchers also examined how promptly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

Industry observers note that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred indicates. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

According to recent reports, by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

Rosamund Pike On Starring in Spiky Stage Drama ‘Inter Alia’: “I Like to Do Things That Are Provocative”

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hollywoodreporter

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before each theatrical run of Inter Alia, Rosamund Pike spends time in court.
  • According to recent reports, she sits in on criminal cases to get a better sense of how the British legal system works, with a particular eye to how female judges act.
  • In preparing to play Jessica Parks, a judge juggling criminal court cases as well as worrying about and taking care of her teenage son, Pike also met with the female judges, as well as with 18-year-old boys to learn how they speak to one another and how they view women.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before each theatrical run of Inter Alia, Rosamund Pike spends time in court.

According to recent reports, she sits in on criminal cases to get a better sense of how the British legal system works, with a particular eye to how female judges act. In one instance, Pike heard a judge reprimand counsel with a stern “I have ruled on that,” and asked playwright Suzie Miller to add that into the script to help give her own character more authenticity and authority.

In preparing to play Jessica Parks, a judge juggling criminal court cases as well as worrying about and taking care of her teenage son, Pike also met with the female judges, as well as with 18-year-old boys to learn how they speak to one another and how they view women. Together, all of these learnings have stayed under the surface for Pike, and helped her bring forward a layered, lived-in portrayal as she approaches the role for a third time and makes her Broadway debut.

According to recent reports, “I wanted there to be humor. I met so many wise, witty, thoughtful, kind female judges. I really wanted to represent them. I wanted it to be as nuanced as we could make it. I wanted the teenage life to be recognizable and current,” Pike mentioned. “And I also, I suppose, the other massive thing is I wanted Jessica to fall on her sword. I wanted her to be so shaken to her core the moral compass she felt was absolute no longer is. “.

It has been revealed that pike first took on the role during the play’s world premiere at London’s National Theatre in 2025. At the time, it had been close to 15 years since the Oscar-nominee had been on stage, after last appearing in Hedda Gabler. She wanted to return in a “modern play that really speaks to now” and finally found that in Miller’s Inter Alia, which demonstrates a woman whose prowess at work adjudicating sexual assault cases and speaking up for women is called into question when her own son is accused of rape.

Sources indicate that “I like to do things that are provocative. I like to do things where people feel glad that they went to the theater, that they got something out of it emotionally, and that they felt something. I go to the theater because I want to feel something, and I want to think differently about things, and then I thought, ‘Well, I think this play might do that,’” remarked Pike, who is also known for her on-screen roles in Gone Girl, Saltburn and Pride and Prejudice.

In a recent development, the play, which had a subsequent West End run before heading to Broadway, is meant to be a kind of sister play to Prima Facie, Miller’s one-woman show which starred Jodie Comer in the West End and on Broadway in 2023. That play followed Comer as a defense barrister who begins by defending men accused of sexual assault and then confronts how the legal system treats women once she is a victim of assault.

While Pike has two fellow actors on stage with her, playing her son and her husband, who is at times loving, and, at times, jealous of her rise at work, much of the show relies on Pike ping-ponging between the naturalistic settings of her home life and speaking to unseen fellow lawyers and others and monologuing to the audience about motherhood and the challenges of raising a son in modern society, as well as revisiting the memory of a former incident with her son as a young child.

“It’s a very unusual play, and I think that’s what Susie handled so deftly was the different sort of threads of a woman’s life and the bits you have narrative control over, and the bits you don’t have narrative control over,” Pike said.

And so while the play has a lot of physical demands, including Pike kicking off the show as the leader of a rock band, Pike notes that it’s been the mental workload that’s been particularly taxing, as her character switches between the naturalistic and imagined worlds.

According to recent reports, the Broadway run began previews Nov. 11, ahead of a Dec. 1 opening. Pike took home a 2026 Olivier Award for her London performance. Combining her research with her experience doing the prior runs has allowed her to move past the technical aspects of the play, like lines and the blocking, into a more fully realized experience.

Sources indicate that “Every step of the way, she has surprised me, made me laugh. She’s incredibly naughty, but fun. She works as hard as anyone I’ve ever met, and she’s sort of relentless in going ‘I want to make this show mean the most it can mean,’” said director Justin Martin, who has been with the play since the beginning.

Her role, and the play itself evolves, he added, in relation to current events.

Speaking ahead of her first preview, news was swirling about an alleged sexual assault in 2024 at a Cornell University fraternity house, which would be the kind of case to come before Pike’s character in the play, and in keeping with the subjects the play raises.

Pike noted that audiences can’t help but bring events like this into the theater with them, which influences their experience of the play. While the text of the play itself doesn’t change, the newspapers on the family’s kitchen table on set show current headlines, which also feeds into their performances and her portrayal as a judge.

Sources indicate that “I think our play affects people very deeply because of all the themes it discusses about family, about motherhood, about raising boys, about responsibility of boys. We’re not going to materially change the play in any way, but that’s what great art can do,” Pike said. “The arts can shed a light or hold a mirror up to our world in a way that is sometimes more truthful and allows us to access those feelings, because sometimes the real event is too close or too confusing for us to actually access an emotional response.”.

According to recent reports, from her own time in British courts, Pike stated she was struck by the way in which she saw a legal system set up to test and sometimes undermine the stories of women who come forward with a rape case, which ends up being another traumatic experience for victims. This play, from Miller, a former lawyer, may help point to the flaws in the system, she notes, in addition to its broader themes about how to bring up boys in modern society.

“I’ve sat in court and watched so many men be found not guilty of sexual assault,” Pike noted. “I think Susie Miller always wants to raise a conversation within the law.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the years, “Meet the Parents” writer John Hamburg would exchange the occasional text or email with his collaborators from the 2000 movie to ask whether anyone had another sequel idea.
  • “It felt like a way back into the story,” says Hamburg, best known for “Zoolander” and “I Love You, Man,” in addition to the “Focker” films.
  • The result is “Focker In-Law,” a battle of wits that plays out as Greg’s son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) brings home his fresh girlfriend, a former FBI hostage negotiator named Olivia (Ariana Grande).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, “Meet the Parents” writer John Hamburg would exchange the occasional text or email with his collaborators from the 2000 movie to ask whether anyone had another sequel idea. (They had already revisited the characters, mismatched in-laws portrayed by Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, to outsized commercial success in 2004’s “Meet the Fockers” and 2010’s “Little Fockers.”) But nothing else stuck — until they realized Stiller was the same age as De Niro’s character in the first film, a comedy about male nurse Gaylord “Greg” Focker who goes through hijinks hell when he’s introduced to his girlfriend’s family, including her intimidating father Jack Byrnes. Related Stories Generative AI Indian Feature 'Maharaja in Denims,' Inspired by Sikh Ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sets April 2027 Release (EXCLUSIVE) Cole Sprouse Says He Didn't Make 'Substantial Money' on 'Riverdale' Until Season 4: TV Is 'Not as Profitable for Actors Anymore'.

“It felt like a way back into the story,” says Hamburg, best known for “Zoolander” and “I Love You, Man,” in addition to the “Focker” films. “Greg Focker finds himself where Jack was all those years ago. What a full-circle moment.”.

The result is “Focker In-Law,” a battle of wits that plays out as Greg’s son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) brings home his fresh girlfriend, a former FBI hostage negotiator named Olivia (Ariana Grande). The new installment, written and directed by Hamburg, takes place as the entire family — including Greg and Jack’s wives Pam and Dina (Teri Polo and Blythe Danner), as well as Greg and Pam’s daughter Samantha (Beanie Feldstein) and her boyfriend Eduardo (Eduardo Franco) — return to Long Island to celebrate Jack’s 80th birthday.

According to recent reports, ahead of the big-screen release — “Focker In-Law” opens in theaters on Nov. 25 — Hamburg spoke to Variety about reconnecting with Stiller and De Niro, Grande’s comedic chops and why Barbra Streisand and Dustin Hoffman didn’t return as Greg’s parents.

It has been revealed that it was surreal. The first time I was at the Byrnes family home in Oyster Bay, Long Island, I was 29, and now I’m coming back in my 50s. That was my first substantial job in the business.

Industry observers note that from time to time, the original group who made the first few movies would text or email to say, “Is there any idea?” But it wasn’t something on my mind. Peter Cramer at Universal was a massive proponent of this movie, and he jump-started it, saying, “We would be interested if you guys would be interested.” We were all driven by one thing: “Do we have a story that we’re excited to tell?” It wasn’t “let’s cash in,” I promise. We all were happy doing other things.

According to recent reports, it was really joyful to be back with those guys. Their chemistry is incredible. The fact that we have this history helps on set. There’s so much trust.

According to recent reports, we knew we needed to bring a big new element to this, just like we had in “Meet the Fockers,” bringing in Dustin Hoffman and Barbra Streisand as Greg’s parents. Ariana was the perfect person. She’s hilarious, and she’s got great timing. I can’t believe she’s been in as few big movies as she has, because she’s so skilled. Bringing her in was this injection of awesomeness. She would light up the set. I really love her energy, and she’s so much fun to be around and to work with — so engaged and committed and professional and early. She was always the first one there.

Oh, they were totally game. Ben Stiller is basically the most committed actor who could ever exist. As long as he thinks it’s right for the story, he will go for it, 100%. The first day of rehearsal — Ben and Ari had met, but they hadn’t rehearsed — was the Heimlich maneuver scene. So it was literally, like, “Ben, Ari — say hi to each other. OK, now you’re gonna get behind Ben and start giving him the Heimlich.” Ari was tentative at first because they didn’t know each other well. And Ben’s like, “Go for it. Don’t worry.” There were no stunt doubles.

According to recent reports, that was a very physical scene. That was crazy to shoot. Ari took the kitchen stuff really seriously and took multiple lessons with a world-class chef to learn knife skills. It was the sous chef of my good friend Dan Barber, who owns Blue Hill at Stone Barns. And then the flame, it wasn’t done all with CGI. There was a special-effects flame that shot up in Ben’s face, and then Ariana was swatting him, and he was pushing back. They were both so in it. Ben was saying, “Swat me in the face,” and Ariana was saying, “Put your hand on my face to push me away!” There was no being shy around each other.

De Niro, at 82 years old, was cruising on that bike. He has this very unique way of riding a bike. His shoulders kind of rock back and forth, and he was super into it. Ariana took lessons to get as proficient as possible on the bike. Ben is a big cyclist, so he slipped into that pretty easily.

In a recent development, bob is a fitness guy. He takes it really seriously. I was talking to his trainer and he was like, “No, Bob hits it hard many days of the week.” But Jack Byrnes is suddenly into wellness in a way he hadn’t been in the previous movies, so Bob got even more ripped and stronger for the role. He went full Jake LaMotta in “Raging Bull.” Bob and Ben knew there was a scene where they were both going to be in speedos, so they’re like, “We gotta go for it.”.

You’d have to ask Bob. I’m not sure, but Bob has kids and grandkids. He’s around young people all the time, so Bob’s pretty hip. I think he knew. He might not let that on, but he’d be like, “I know, John. I know.”.

In a recent development, look, I have no one to blame but myself. I wrote that line. Maybe there’s more to mine, but only if it’s organic and feels like there’s a reason for it to exist. Talk to me after Thanksgiving weekend.

I have some people in mind, but there’s no way I could talk about this right now.

It has been revealed that I was a fan of Cole’s, and flight attendants are very vital in these movies. Rachel Tenner, our casting director, was like, “What about Cole Escola?” Immediately, my producers and I were like, “That would be perfect.” Cole might be one of the funniest human beings I’ve ever been around, and they made Ben and Ariana die laughing for those three days that they were on set.

It has been revealed that I wanted to bring back the lie detector, because that’s such an notable part of the franchise. And now we have Olivia Jones, who is FBI, so she might know her way around a lie detector. You’re probably going to have a dinner table scene. The dinner table scene in the first movie ends in such a funny way, with Greg breaking the urn of Jack’s mom and Jinx [the cat] peeing on the ashes. I don’t know that we’re ever going to top that, but what can we do that will take the audience by surprise and feel right for the story? So I wrote the part with Greg baby-birding Grandpa Jack. It’s a pretty epic moment. My fellow filmmakers on this movie were a little skeptical, and I’m wrong about a lot of stuff, but I was like, “Guys, I feel it in my gut. This is gonna work.”.

It has been revealed that that’s really notable, because it’s been a long time since “Meet the Parents.” I have to assume that many people aren’t that familiar, or maybe they saw it a long time ago. I wanted to make this movie work if you’d never seen any of the “Meet the Parents,” as a funny, heartfelt, character-based comedy. But then, of course, it is a “Meet the Parents” movie, so there’s going to be certain touchstones. My job was finding fresh ways in.

Yes, of course. They were so incredible in “Meet the Fockers.” But I wanted to bring it back to the simplicity of the original “Meet the Parents.” Dustin and Barbra are so iconic that I didn’t want to bring them back in a smaller part if I couldn’t service their characters, because I had all these new characters. If I brought them back, I would have to take away from Olivia, Henry, Samantha and Eduardo. It was a hard choice. Not that they would have agreed to come back. But for this story, it didn’t feel like the movie could hold all of that. But maybe in a fifth one….

It has been revealed that it’s got to be the writing. No, I’m just kidding. If you use that quote, you have to say I was joking. I believe it’s because the themes are relatable and timeless. Everybody, at one point in their lives, is probably going to introduce their significant other to their families.

As far as making the movie, it wasn’t that different. Universal gave us so much support. One thing is studios literally stopped making this type of comedy for theaters. It’s hard to point to the last one. I’m not talking about hilarious movies like the “Naked Gun” or “Scary Movie” reboots. Those are a little different, because they’re in their own sub-genre. But the movies I made or watched in the ’90s and 2000s stopped getting made. They moved to streaming, which can be great, but it’s just different. I think people were missing that communal feeling of being in a theater with hundreds of people and sharing laughter at cringe moments.

Power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses and residential buildings: The massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under fire, affecting German companies.

According to recent reports, "Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).

At the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

Industry observers note that according to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs mentioned. "We are preparing for a difficult winter.".

After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.

"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks.".

According to recent reports, energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.

Industry observers note that "Not a single German tech giant has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, military cooperation currently tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but upcoming capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine and the software in Germany.

According to recent reports, A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz stated.

The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," he said.

According to recent reports, for foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act. On the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following 10 years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.

In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.

"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi said in Berlin.

According to recent reports, "German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted. However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks.".

Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he added.

At the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment.".

Sources indicate that another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.

In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: Companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the firm and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different. When investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.

This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.

It has been revealed that german companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

The automaker remarked Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

Sources indicate that the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

Recent findings suggest that the automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

Sources indicate that "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke remarked Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

It has been revealed that in September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

According to recent reports, ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the tech giant's energy storage business. That's down from initial prepares of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has noted the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford stated it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it prepares to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

  • In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”.

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet revealed whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey.

According to recent reports, “It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”.

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

It has been revealed that the accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It presently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

Industry observers note that the HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” noted Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party revealed support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake.

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” mentioned Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”.

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, noted Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”.

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” remarked Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”.

Ozsoy indicates his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

According to recent reports, “We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker noted.

Two women arrested for not wearing hijab following ‘yogurt attack’.

Two women were arrested in Iran for failing to wear the hijab in public, after a man threw a tub of yogurt at them at a store in the city of Shandiz on Thursday, according to Mizan News Agency, the state-run outlet for Iran’s judiciary.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

Oil prices spiked Monday after OPEC+ producers unexpectedly announced that they would cut output. Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped 5.31% to $84.13 a barrel, while WTI, the US benchmark, rose 5.48% to $79.83. Both were the sharpest price rises in almost a year. The collective output cut by the nine members of OPEC+ totals 1.66 million barrels per day.

Iran blames Israel for the killing of second IRGC officer, vows to respond.

Recent findings suggest that A second Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) officer died following an attack in Syria on Friday, according to Iranian state media on Sunday. Iranian state media mentioned the Iranian military adviser died after an Israeli attack near the Syrian capital Damascus left him wounded. The attack also killed another IRGC officer. In a tweet on Sunday, Iranian government spokesman Ali Bahadori Jahromi said the alleged Israeli attack wouldn’t go unanswered. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Nasser Kanaani said on Sunday that Iran has the right to respond to “state terrorism.”.

Iranian-American comedian Maz Jobrani, who has been touring the Middle East, spoke to CNN’s Becky Anderson about his support for the protests in his homeland, saying that he used his standup comedy platform to highlight the “brutality against the Iranian people.”.

“It was an opportunity for me to say, ‘let’s keep fighting,’” he noted.

An Iranian state news outlet is gloating at what it sees as the demise of the US dollar.

IRNA recreated a popular meme to mark China and Brazil’s decision to reportedly ditch the US dollar as an intermediary in trade, citing the Chinese state news outlet, China Daily. It demonstrates two men representing China and Brazil posing in front of a grave labelled “USD.”.

The meme was pinned to the top of IRNA’s Twitter page, and was met with laughter and ridicule. “Dream on,” remarked another user, pointing to the dollar’s use as the main reserve currency around the world.

Breaking: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions?
  • Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA.
  • Industry observers note that the research was led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

Industry observers note that the research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists.

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An crucial difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Industry observers note that why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage.

According to recent reports, the results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an crucial advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," noted Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.".

In a recent development, this finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an key role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

Fresh Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection.

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

According to recent reports, the team established a latest set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," noted Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team plan to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins.".

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

Industry News: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that at an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today.
  • The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes.
  • In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve notable biological functions.

In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation.

It has been revealed that one of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

It has been revealed that they found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

It has been revealed that this research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

Sources indicate that "We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," remarked Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject.".

In a recent development, gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," stated Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

Industry observers note that he added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.".

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island.

Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

It has been revealed that he arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

In a recent development, today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time ever, a foreign astronaut has set foot inside China's Tiangong space station.

That pioneer is Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who arrived at Tiangong aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft early this morning (Nov. 25).

"The Chinese space station is always something to look forward to!" the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) wrote in an update today (in Mandarin; translation by Google). "China's 'Tiangong' welcomes partners from all over the world to visit!".

According to recent reports, ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces, is a payload specialist on Shenzhou-24. He found his way onto the mission thanks to a space-cooperation agreement that China signed with Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025.

Ali and his two Shenzhou-24 crewmates — commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi — enjoyed a short and smooth ride to their orbital destination. They lifted off atop a Long March 2F rocket on Tuesday (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT on Nov. 25) and reached Tiangong a little over six hours later.

Sources indicate that tang and Wu will live aboard the outpost for the usual six-month stint. Ali, however, will come home in just a week, hitching a ride with two of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong in May.

Ali will be busy during his short space stay, conducting a set of joint Chinese-Pakistani experiments.

"Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, with Ali also scheduled to conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria," The Times of India wrote today.

Recent findings suggest that the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain on the station until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore set a Chinese record, becoming the first astronaut from his country to live in low Earth orbit for a full year.

Astronauts from the Soviet Union/Russia and the United States have already blazed this long-duration trail. The global record for longest continuous space stay is 437 days, set by cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov aboard the Mir space station from January 1994 to March 1995.

Ali is not the first person from Pakistan ever to reach space, by the way. That distinction belongs to adventurer Namira Salim, who traveled to suborbital space on a tourism flight with Virgin Galactic in October 2023.

According to recent reports, shenzhou-24 is the 12th crewed mission to Tiangong, a three-module, T-shaped outpost that China finished assembling in late 2022. Well, "finished" might not be the right term; China intends to expand Tiangong, which is at the moment about 20% as massive as the International Space Station.

‘Gugu’s World’ Team on the Diversity of Brazilian Cinema and Championing Films That ‘Respect the Storyteller’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The creative team behind the coming-of-age drama celebrates a long journey that has culminated in making a star out of newcomer Yuri Gomes and connecting with audiences across Brazil and the world.
  • In the nine months since “Gugu’s World” premiered in Berlin, director Allan Deberton has had only the most “joyful experiences.” By the time the filmmaker sits down with Variety to discuss the whirlwind, the film has just opened in its home country of Brazil, turning its young star into a phenomenon.
  • That star is Yuri Gomes, who plays the titular Gugu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The creative team behind the coming-of-age drama celebrates a long journey that has culminated in making a star out of newcomer Yuri Gomes and connecting with audiences across Brazil and the world.

In the nine months since “Gugu’s World” premiered in Berlin, director Allan Deberton has had only the most “joyful experiences.” By the time the filmmaker sits down with Variety to discuss the whirlwind, the film has just opened in its home country of Brazil, turning its young star into a phenomenon.

That star is Yuri Gomes, who plays the titular Gugu. The boy is the epitome of freedom, zigzagging across a dirt field with a football, then breaking into a dance sequence the moment he hears the throbbing beats of Brazilian brega music. Yes, those around him judge him, including stern dad Batista (Lázaro Ramos), but Gugu is sheltered by the love of grandmother Dilma (Teca Pereira). The two live together in a small town in Ceará, their loving home and safe cocoon until the day Dilma’s health deteriorates due to a rapidly developing case of Alzheimer’s. Related Stories Michael Urie to Host 79th Writers Guild Awards in New York (EXCLUSIVE) MasterClass Courses -- From Spike Lee, Mark Cuban and Martha Stewart -- Are 50% Off This Black Friday.

Sources indicate that “Gugu’s World” follows Deberton’s “Pacarrete” and reunites the director with screenwriter André Araújo, who originated the story. The tale of this energetic boy resonated deeply with the filmmaker, who knew he needed a “great cast” to do justice to the “responsibility” of tackling the issues in the script, from talking about young queerness to dealing with caring responsibilities and progressive disorders. Deberton landed two of Brazil’s great screen stars in Ramos and Pereira, but the process of finding Gugu was a much more complex, lengthy operation. The film team saw over 700 kids and eventually found Gomes, a star-in-the-making.

Recent findings suggest that “We needed an actor who had the spirit of Gugu,” claims producer Karen Castanho of Biônica Filmes. “But today, the great challenge of filming kids is that, because of social media, kids are not very spontaneous. Yuri is the opposite of that.”.

According to recent reports, deberton worked closely with casting director and AD Luciana Vieira to ensure that not only Gomes but the wider cast of children were “very natural.” “We simply see children being children. We don’t see kids acting. I think that’s very strong in the film.”.

Recent findings suggest that the director said it is “transformative” to work with children. He enjoyed the experience so much that he decided to replicate it for his next project, “Adoption,” dealing with his personal experience adopting his son. “What they put on the screen is very truthful. We need to be open to that gaze, which is pure, intimate, truthful and that makes us feel alive.”.

The film presented a great challenge to Ramos, an actor-director with decades of experience and one of the most recognizable names in Brazil thanks to his work on telenovelas and films such as “Madame Satã” and “Carandiru.” Ramos is more widely known for his loving, well-humored roles, so playing a stern father dealing with internalized homophobia and unable to accept his son was difficult.

Sources indicate that “My first read of [Batista] was one that is very distant from the dad I aim to be,” he remarked. “I was looking to villainize that figure, to signal his flaws, like an alert call. But when we started rehearsing, he gained richness and a much more interesting personality, which is this man who does care about his child, who seeks to be closer to his child, but he doesn’t have the resources.”.

It has been revealed that asked about the physicality of his character, who is often contained in contrast to Gugu’s penchant for movement, Ramos shared the complex process. During rehearsals, it felt “curious” to Ramos how he couldn’t mimic Gomes’ movements. The two often danced together or moved together between takes, but Ramos returned to introspection when cameras rolled. “It was good to encounter that vitality of his to understand the opposition we’d aim for in each scene,” he mentioned.

Pereira, on the other hand, was able to imbue Dilma with a lot of herself, such as “her joy for life, that animated way of living and the way she cares for her grandson,” she noted. The role was still quite different from everything she had done previously, with the experience made even more special thanks to the relationship she developed with Gomes. “Luciana Vieira gave us exercises for us to develop that care, to develop a bond,” she recalled. “It was great. Yuri is an intelligent, clever child, as well as talented.”.

Working on an indie project always brings a set of challenges, but shooting with a large ensemble cast mostly of children and setting the production in Quixadá, a small city in the inland of Ceará, added massively to Castanho’s plate.

Despite the city being a frequent production hub, the film team wanted to avoid “obvious locations,” turning the city into a base camp. “Most of the locations were within one hour of the city, with a massive team, to sets without any infrastructure. We had to literally bring everything to film in these places, which involved traveling one hour every day.”.

Recent findings suggest that “At the same time, we needed a city that could host all these people,” added the producer. “The logistical challenge was huge. The background actors are all from the region, but the team is very diverse. Brazil is a country of continental dimensions; we had professionals from all over Brazil. The greatest challenge for us was logistical.”.

Industry observers note that deberton noted that the local population completely embraced the project, and the film team worked closely with all background extras to ensure they were comfortable with the costume and production design and felt integrated into the production. Ramos remarked he “loves shooting on location” and ended up staying longer in Quixadá than he was originally supposed to. “I live in an urban center, I’m very agitated, very rushed,” he said. “And there’s a timing there of the effect of a smaller city, where people know each other, where people have time to chat and I think that ended up influencing me too.”.

According to recent reports, when asked what “Gugu’s World” communicates about Brazil to international audiences and what they want the film to be in dialogue with when it meets audiences all over the world, the team Castanho is quick to say she wants people to understand the diversity of Brazilian cinema. “This is a small film with a big heart and, especially in this moment in the world, I think we all need that love.”.

Deberton echoes that thought, saying he often felt that Brazilian films were “put in a box” as a type of cinema that would connect with cinephiles but not broad audiences. “I think it’s the opposite: when we have access to powerful stories, to characters that transform, that connection happens naturally and genuinely with the audience,” he remarked.

“This progress that we’re seeing with national cinema highlights a quality of directors, of teams and producers,” added Pereira, noting the great momentum of her national cinema, with standout international hits such as “I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent” projecting Brazilian films to the world.

Industry observers note that “As Allan indicates, regionality is very important because we don’t want to stay just in the substantial urban centers,” added the actress. “The quality of the work depends also on the opportunities. Brazil is very diverse. We have a lot to show still, and a lot to do still … And for me it’s very important. I want and hope that all this results in more jobs for many people, because we need to talk about ourselves. And that should be seen by the whole world.”.

Ramos wrapped the conversation by humorously stating he would bring a “contentious” subject to the table, which is the need for the regulation of streamers in Brazil so that independent productions can benefit from the market they have helped build, as well as revising how partnerships with major studios and production companies are forged.

Sources indicate that “After the pandemic, we went through a period in which, due to market needs, we made some concessions and negotiations, and made many films without identity,” he said. “People watched a film and wouldn’t even know the name of the protagonist at the end of the movie. Or they would be faced with a storytelling model based on either an algorithm or on the desires of another country.”.

Industry observers note that “Gugu’s World” goes against the grain in this sense, according to the veteran performer. “This film struggled to find partners and financiers for a long time,” he went on. “So let’s take the opportunity to get people to consider the current state of filmmaking, watch this film and go back to respecting the storyteller, which I think is an vital message, because otherwise we get a lot of tepid or similar movies.”.

Industry News: CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has unveiled that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

It has been revealed that "The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed.".

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.".

The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win.".

According to recent reports, "I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.

Industry observers note that "African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything.".

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

Industry observers note that the country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.

Sources indicate that although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.
